activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York on March 25, 1911, killed 146 garment workers, many trapped because exit doors had been locked.
story:
The warehouse had a smell Connor decided was ancient cardboard, sweetish and damp, and on his first shift the supervisor handed him a box cutter and pointed at a pallet of returns. His job was to open each carton, scan its contents and shelve it, which meant learning the building's taxonomy by walking it: electronics along the north wall, then a whole phylum of kitchen goods, small appliances evolving into cookware, until near the back the shelves gave up entirely and the floor became a plain of boxes stacked almost to the rafters. It was the boxes that bothered him. Not the boxes themselves, but where they were, in front of a steel door with a green EXIT sign burning above it.

He had a want, and it was simple: tuition money for September, a few thousand dollars saved by the end of summer. The warehouse paid four dollars an hour more than the grocery store where his friend Vivienne worked, which he'd assumed was because of the night shift. But his second week, a man named Loic, who had worked there eleven years and could palletize a truck in his sleep, corrected him over lunch. "Night premium's a dollar," Loic said. "The rest is the contract. We're unionized. Went on strike for six days in 2019, my first year, and the overtime after forty hours and the safety language all came out of that." He said safety language like it was a phrase from scripture. "Breaks, too. Legally you get some of that anyway. Labour law sets the floor. The contract's what we built on top of it."

Connor filed this away the way he filed everything that summer, but the exit door kept surfacing in his mind. Mr. Bélanger had covered it in history class in the spring, and Connor hadn't even needed to study it for the test; the image had done the work on its own. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York, on March 25, 1911. One hundred and forty-six garment workers died, many of them trapped because the exit doors had been locked. He remembered Vivienne, two rows over, saying quietly, "Locked so they couldn't take breaks," and Mr. Bélanger nodding once and moving on, because he trusted them to carry the weight of it themselves.

On Thursday the aisle was worse. Someone had parked a recalcitrant pallet jack crosswise, its wheel seized, and cases of glassware rose around it like a wall. Connor stood there with his scanner going cold in his hand. He thought about saying nothing. He was seventeen, three weeks into the job, and the supervisor had a rhythm to his voice that suggested questions were an interruption to it. He also thought about the fact that Loic walked past this door forty times a night and had stopped seeing it, the way you stop seeing a crack in your own ceiling.

He went and found Loic first, at the loading dock, and asked, quietly, whether the safety language in the contract covered exits. Loic set down his clipboard. "It's in the Occupational Safety rules too, federal and provincial. Means of egress has to stay clear. Why." Connor led him back and watched eleven years of seeing return to the man's face. "Merde," Loic said, and then, without any ceremony, began to exhume the door, lifting cases two at a time, passing them to Connor, who stacked them in the empty bay beside the aisle. It took them most of a break they weren't required to give up, and when the door was visible down to its threshold, Loic wiped his hands and studied it as if confirming a rumour. At the next contract negotiation, he said, they'd ask for painted floor markings and a written fine for blocked egress. The company would counter, they'd meet somewhere in the middle, and the middle would inch forward, the way it always did.

The supervisor appeared at the end of the aisle while they were repositioning the pallet jack. He looked at the clear door, at the two of them sweating, and something crossed his face that Connor couldn't fully read, irritation layered over something that might have been shame. "Inventory got ahead of us," the supervisor said, which wasn't an apology and wasn't a lie. Loic said they'd flagged it, in front of a witness, and the supervisor said he'd have maintenance fix the jack by Monday.

Connor worked until two in the morning, then rode his bike home through streets that smelled of cut grass. He still didn't know whether the supervisor would have cared if he'd reported the door up the chain instead of going to Loic, or whether the union would actually win the markings at the table, or whether he, Connor, had done something brave or only something any person would do. The summer would answer some of that and not the rest. But he stopped at the corner by the all-night bakery, where the light was on, and texted Vivienne a single line.

"Got the job with the fire doors unlocked," he wrote, and waited for the three dots to appear.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
The Tuesday after her econ teacher announced the oral exam, Lea volunteered to close the bookshop alone, mostly so she could stand behind the register with the flashcards Ms. Sutton kept under the till and talk to herself without anyone watching. The exam required her to explain, in plain language, why a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She understood the chain in theory. She could not yet say it out loud without feeling like she was reciting a spell.

"Raise rates, borrowing costs more, so people take fewer loans, so they spend less, so prices stop climbing so fast," she told the espresso machine. It sounded like a shopping list.

At nine Sasha came in through the back door, still in her volleyball warmups, and dropped onto the stool behind the returns desk. Sasha wanted Saturday off. She had a tournament in the city, a real one, scouts allegedly attending, and she wanted Lea to take both weekend shifts in exchange for a favor she described only as "something big, I promise, I'm working on it."

"Saturday's when Neveah and I do the practice exam at the library," Lea said. "You know that."

"You're reticent about the favor, I get it, but that's exactly why you should say yes. Mystery is a currency."

"That's not what reticent means in a sentence and you know it." Lea slid the flashcards across the counter. "Actually, sit there. You're my practice dummy. I have to explain inflation to a person, not a wall."

Sasha groaned but straightened, resting her chin on her fist like a hostile school board. "Fine. Convince me."

Lea began with the chain, but this time she reached for a picture. If money is cheap to borrow, everyone's buying, and when everyone's buying, sellers can charge more, so prices rise. Make money expensive and the crowd thins out; sellers can't push prices on a crowd that isn't there. Sasha kept interrupting with edge cases, what about people with savings, what about wages, and Lea found herself saying, more than once, "that's real, and it's the part I can't resolve yet," because it was. The textbook made it sound frictionless. Her mother's rent going up last spring had not been frictionless.

"Okay," Sasha said, "but why do you trust the central bank to get the number right at all? Who decided they could just pick a target?"

Lea didn't know. She'd assumed inflation targeting was ancient, like something carved into the founding of banking, and she said so. Sasha got out her phone, typed with her thumbs, and then held the screen up like a verdict.

"New Zealand," she read. "New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent."

"Nineteen ninety," Lea repeated. "That's after Ms. Sutton started working."

Ms. Sutton, locking the front door behind a last customer, raised an eyebrow at her own name. "After I started working, what?"

"Nothing," Lea said, though she was already copying the date onto the back of a receipt. It unsettled her pleasantly that the whole system was younger than the woman who owned the shop, that somebody had invented it, had sat in a room and argued over a range of 0 to 2 percent, and that other countries had watched and copied. It made the exam answer feel less like physics and more like a decision people were still living inside.

She worked it into her explanation on the spot, using Sasha as the examiner again. "So when people ask whether central banks have always aimed at a set number, no, they haven't. New Zealand did it first, March 1990." Sasha made her repeat the range twice, claimed the first telling had drifted into pedantry, "0 to 2 percent, say it exactly," and made her say it a third time until it came out clean.

Lea covered the Saturday morning shift. She decided it on the walk home, weighing the exam against Sasha's tournament, and concluded that she could practice on a bus as well as in a library, and that Sasha's whole reticent "something big" was probably just a thank-you she was too proud to name in advance. She texted her the answer before she could soften it. Sunday afternoon Sasha appeared at the shop with a bakery box and a laminated diagram of the interest rate chain, arrows drawn in green marker, one box circled where she'd written "the part Lea says is real but unresolved."

"What's this for?"

"For your exam," Sasha said. "And there's no big favor. I just didn't want to say thank you before it was done." She set the box on the counter and pointed at it. "Eat one before you open the till."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The portal refreshed itself at 3:14 on a Thursday afternoon, and Victoria watched the status line change from "application complete" to "waitlist offered" without any ceremony at all. She sat at her mother's desk in the corner of the living room, the good lamp burning beside the keyboard, and read the sentence four times. The committee had been impressed. The committee encouraged her to remain interested. The committee could not, at this time, offer admission.

She called Maeva, who was still at soccer practice, and then Dillon, who answered on the second ring with his mouth full of something.

"Waitlisted," she said. "At Aldercott."

There was a swallowing noise, and then Dillon said, "That's basically a maybe."

"It's basically a no," Victoria said. "With manners."

She opened a second tab and typed the words herself, because she wanted to arrive at the mechanics on her own terms rather than have them handed to her. The results were forums, mostly, seniors in other years asking the same question in different fonts. She learned that many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. It was a matter of arithmetic, not mercy. Nobody decided anything until the deposits were counted, and the deposits were counted in May, and May was five weeks away.

"Okay," she said out loud, to the lamp. "So I wait."

Except that she couldn't only wait, because the state university an hour from her house wanted a deposit by the first of May, and the deposit was three hundred dollars, nonrefundable, and her mother had put the money in an envelope in the silverware drawer three days ago like it was a birthday card. Victoria knew it was there. She had looked at the envelope twice while getting a spoon.

Maeva came over that evening with her practice bag still smelling of grass and sat cross-legged on the floor beside the desk chair. "So what's the actual problem? You got into the state school. Most people would just be happy."

"The problem is three hundred dollars," Victoria said. "I send it, and then Aldercott calls in May and I'm in, and the money's gone, and my mother's out three hundred dollars for a school I don't attend. Or I don't send it, and Aldercott calls, and I have nowhere to sit in September because I gambled."

"That's grim."

"It's a dichotomy," Victoria said. "My grandmother would say I'm dichotomizing. Two boxes, no third option. She uses that word whenever anyone in the family pretends there are only two choices, which is apparently a family trait."

"And is she right? Are there only two?"

Victoria pulled up the FAQ page from Aldercott again. The word "waitlist" appeared eleven times, which she counted, and she was explaining to Maeva that nobody at the college would tell her anything personal, no hint of her position on the list, when Maeva leaned over and pointed at the deposit deadline on the other screen.

"First of May," Maeva read. "And you said they fill spots in May, after the deposits are in. So it's a race, kind of. You pay on the last possible day and hope the phone rings before your money does something permanent."

"The last possible day," Victoria said slowly, "is a third box."

"Your grandmother would be proud."

Dillon arrived at nine with two coffees and his own putative expertise, gathered, he admitted, from a cousin who had been waitlisted at a school in Ohio four years ago and never gotten off the list. He delivered this pedigree with real authority, and Victoria let him, because the coffee was good and because his cousin's failure was a useful data point even secondhand.

"So you're sending it," Dillon said. "The deposit. That's what my cousin did, and she ended up fine at the state school anyway."

"She ended up fine," Victoria agreed. "But she never had to choose between the two of them. I might."

She filled out the state university's enrollment form that night while Maeva read questions aloud and Dillon looked up the housing deadlines, which were, he announced with some vindication, also in May. Everything was in May. The whole architecture of the spring seemed designed so that nobody would know anything until the last permissible moment, a system built entirely on other people's deposits arriving before yours could be returned.

Her mother came home at eleven and stood behind the chair with her coat still on, reading the screen over Victoria's shoulder. "So you're going to the state school," she said.

"I'm buying a ticket to the state school," Victoria said. "Whether I ride the train is a different question."

"That's the most expensive sentence you've ever said."

"I know."

Her mother took the envelope out of the silverware drawer and set it beside the keyboard, and Victoria entered the card number, and the confirmation page loaded slowly, the little wheel turning in the middle of the screen while nobody in the room moved. Then it cleared, and the words "Thank you, Victoria" came up in cheerful blue type, already addressed to her as if the decision were final, as if the words on the page were not, themselves, still waiting.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Chinese New Year's Eve reunion dinner, fish is traditionally served because the word for fish, 'yu', sounds like the word for surplus or abundance.
story:
Olivia had volunteered before she understood what she was volunteering for. Ms. Dlamini, who coordinated the temple's community kitchen every year, had asked who would lead the New Year's Eve reunion dinner this time, since Olivia's grandmother's hands had begun to shake too badly to hold a cleaver, and Olivia had raised her hand in the fluorescent hush of the meeting hall, thinking mostly that it would be unkind, in that room, to let the silence go on.

Now it was the afternoon before the eve, and the temple's back kitchen smelled of star anise and damp stone. Her task that morning had been to transcribe her grandmother's recipes from a folder of receipts, ticket stubs and letters written across three decades, the ink fading from blue to grey wherever water had touched it. The fish recipe took longest, because her grandmother had written it four different ways on four different scraps, and Olivia sat at the steel counter with a pencil, deciding which version was true.

The fish itself was the problem. Ms. Dlamini had ordered one whole carp from the market, as always, but it had come back with a clouded eye and a smell that Prince, arriving with crates of oranges for the altar, identified immediately. "That is not food," he said, holding the bag at arm's length. "That is a warning." There was no time to return to the market before the temple closed for sweeping, and every family arriving the next evening would expect the dinner her grandmother had cooked for thirty years, complete and correct.

Olivia considered leaving the fish off. There would be dumplings, noodles, the braised mushrooms, eight dishes in all, surely enough. She was halfway through deciding this when she found, folded inside an envelope from 1994, a note in her grandmother's hand: a menu for a reunion dinner with a small drawing of a fish and, beneath it, the words that unlocked the rest. Yu, her grandmother had written, sounds like surplus. Abundance. She had underlined it twice, the way she underlined things that were not suggestions.

Ilias, who had come to help carry tables and had stayed to shell peanuts he had not been asked to shell, read the note over Olivia's shoulder. "So the fish can't be left off," he said slowly. "The word for fish sounds like the word for surplus." Olivia nodded, and the decision she had been half-making came apart in her hands. It was not that eight dishes were not enough. It was that a dinner without the fish would be a different kind of dinner, one that said something she did not mean to say, and she could not pretend otherwise just because the carp had gone bad.

Ms. Dlamini drove to her cousin's fish stall across town, past the shuttered market, and came back after dark with two smaller sea bass packed in ice, refusing payment for the second one. "One year my mother had only a dried fish," she said, laying them out. "You steam it, you place it whole on the platter, you don't apologize for it. Nobody wants an apology at a reunion dinner." Olivia noticed that Ms. Dlamini's coat was wet at the shoulders, that she had gone out into the sleet without an umbrella, and said nothing about it, only set the kettle on for tea.

On the evening itself, the temple hall filled with folding tables and paper lanterns, forty people talking over the sound of the rice cooker. Olivia's grandmother sat at the head table with her shaking hands folded, and when the fish arrived, steamed with ginger and scallions, placed whole and facing the eldest, she looked at it for a long moment before she looked at Olivia. Prince leaned toward Ilias and said, in the tone of someone making a scientific claim, that whoever took the last piece of fish was being altruistic, and therefore a fool, and then took the last piece himself and put it in the grandmother's bowl.

Between carrying dishes and refilling tea, Olivia kept the checklist in her head, ticking through her grandmother's scraps one by one, the order of courses, the fish laid whole, the noodles left uncut. She knew now why the fish mattered, and she knew, too, that she could not fully separate what she believed from what she was performing, that some of the ceremony lived in her hands and some of it lived only in her grandmother's memory, which was already letting certain things go. Later, when the tables were cleared and the oranges from the altar were being handed out for the walk home, her grandmother reached up and touched the sleeve of Olivia's cardigan, and said, "Next year you won't need the papers."

Olivia said, "I'll keep them anyway."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Johann Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel.
story:
The metronome had been her grandfather's, a walnut pyramid with a brass pendulum, and it sat on the piano at home like a small official who had outlived the government that appointed him. Annabelle had ignored it all year, but now the spring recital was three weeks away and Ms. Grewal had said, in that mild voice that made criticism land harder, that her Chopin waltz was "generous with tempo." Rushing, in other words. She had argued, a little, that rushing was a kind of feeling, and Ms. Grewal had said, "Then learn to feel it on purpose," and sent her home with instructions to practice with a beat.

She wound the metronome and set the sliding weight to 120, and the pendulum swung, tick, tick, tick, impervious to her opinions about it. She lasted eight bars before she pulled ahead of it, and then, humiliated, fell behind. It occurred to her that she had never once wondered who had built such a thing, or when, or why a machine should get to decide what a waltz wanted.

Quinten came over that evening, ostensibly to study for the chemistry final, actually to eat the good crackers and lie across her bed. He poked the pendulum with one finger and set it ticking. "Who invented this little guy?"

"I don't know. It was my grandfather's." She had assumed it was older than the house, older than everything. "Probably some German. Everything about pianos is German."

"You could look it up."

"I'm not going to look it up, I'm going to play with it, that's the whole assignment." But the question metastasized through her practice session, spreading from the metronome to the piano itself to the tuning fork in the drawer, and finally, at eleven, she sat cross-legged on the floor with her laptop and found that she had been almost right. Johann Maelzel had patented the mechanical metronome in 1815, drawing on a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel. She read it twice, partly because she was tired and partly because the shape of it pleased her. Maelzel got the patent. Winkel had the design. One man built the thing and another man got his name on it, and two hundred years later a girl on a bedroom floor knew only the name, until tonight.

From the hallway, her mother watched her copy the sentence into the margin of her sheet music, beside a measure she kept fumbling. Annabelle didn't notice her, which was rare. She was saying something under her breath, and her mother caught "Winkel" and "Maelzel" and the word "unfair," and then Annabelle set the pendulum swinging again and played the passage at 60, then 80, then 100, each time slower than she wanted, her shoulders dropping an inch with every repetition. The sound through the doorway was uneven, the machine's tick steady as a heartbeat against the girl's stumbling pulse, and her mother thought, not for the first time, that the piano had been a good inheritance from a man none of them had been able to please.

At school the next day, Annabelle cornered Quinten by the vending machines. "Winkel," she said. "Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel had the design, but Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815. So Maelzel's the name everybody knows."

"Okay," said Quinten. "Is that on the chem final?"

"It's on my conscience." She explained, hands moving, that she'd spent a year treating the metronome as an enemy, an authority to be resented, and that now she couldn't decide whether to resent Maelzel for taking credit or admire Winkel for making the thing anyway. "If you invent something and somebody else patents it, do you stop inventing?"

"Probably you sue him."

"There wasn't time for suing, there was a waltz to learn." Mederic, who had been eavesdropping while pretending to buy chips, asked what a metronome even was, and she demonstrated against the vending machine with a pen, ticking, and he said it sounded like a clock that thought it was better than you, and she laughed harder than the joke deserved.

She kept working at it that week, and something shifted that she could not quite name. The tick stopped being a cage and started being a floor to stand on. When she played with it, she could hear exactly where her rushing began, which turned out to be the same phrase every time, the one her fingers loved too much to let finish. When she played without it, she found she could still hear it, the way you can hear a friend's voice in an empty room. Whether Winkel would have wanted it that way, whether he minded that his name survived only in footnotes, whether credit or the thing itself mattered more, she honestly did not know, and she decided she was allowed not to know, at least until after the recital.

On the night of the recital, before she left, she wound the metronome one turn and set the weight low, and let it tick in the empty living room behind her while she carried her sheet music out to the car. From the driveway, through the window, she could see the small brass pendulum still swinging, patient and exact, keeping time for no one.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
Samuel spread the graph paper across the picnic table and weighted its corners with hockey pucks, because the backyard wind in October had opinions about careful work. He was building a weekly training program for basketball, his first real one, with columns for Monday through Sunday and rows for drills, and he had promised Ms. Nikolaidis, who coached the community league, that he would show her something coherent by Sunday night. The problem was the rest of it. She had said, "Plan the work, but plan the recovery too," and then walked off toward her car before he could ask what that meant, exactly, in rows and columns.

Giuseppe arrived over the fence the way he always did, without preamble, holding a bag of dried apricots he had no intention of sharing. He leaned over the table and squinted at the grid. "You've got shooting drills Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday," he said. "Ladder work Wednesday. What's Saturday?"

"Nothing. That's the point."

"Nothing," Giuseppe repeated, as though Samuel had proposed a religion he'd never heard of.

Samuel explained, as much to himself as to Giuseppe, that he'd read about periodization, about how bodies adapted under stress and then needed the stress withdrawn. He was improvising; the articles he'd found were written for college athletes, and he was sixteen and got his exercise mostly from a bent rim mounted on the garage. Still, he liked the idea that rest could be scheduled with the same seriousness as sprints. He wrote REST in careful capitals across the Saturday row and drew a box around it, and the box looked almost official, almost like something a person with a plan would make.

Abhijot came through the side gate an hour later with his own agenda: a stopwatch and a clipboard and the news that the interminable wait for team announcements was over, that tryouts had been moved up a week, and that only two spots were open for guards. He wanted to film Samuel shooting free throws, ten per set, so they could track percentages the way the serious programs did. Samuel agreed before he had finished agreeing, and that was his first mistake, though he didn't know it yet.

They shot into the grey afternoon until the ball became a sound more than an object, thud and clang against the fading rim. Abhijot called out numbers. Samuel's first set was eight out of ten, which felt like a lie he had accidentally told. His second was seven. His third dropped to six, and his legs, which had carried the morning's ladder drills, began filing complaints he chose to ignore. He had inured himself to tiredness over years of school mornings, and he mistook that numbness for capacity, which was the deeper mistake.

"The wind," Giuseppe offered from the bench.

"There's no wind," Abhijot said, still writing.

At the kitchen table that night, past midnight, Samuel filled in the warm-up row. He researched dynamic stretching, the kind done moving, and wrote it above every session, Monday through Friday, because Ms. Nikolaidis had told him once that cold muscles were how seasons ended. He read about mobility drills and core activation, and somewhere near one in the morning he found a study from Stanford, 2011, about basketball players. It said the players had aimed for ten hours in bed every night, and that their free-throw average had risen from 7.9 successful shots out of 10 to 8.8. He read the sentence three times. Then he looked at the clock in the lower corner of his screen, which read 2:04.

Here was the thing he had not told anyone, not Giuseppe with his apricots, not Abhijot with his clipboard, not even the graph paper. For eleven nights running, he had been up past two, designing programs, watching film, drawing boxes around the word REST. He had been scheduling rest for a body he was refusing to let rest. The study sat on his screen like a mirror angled to catch him, and he thought of his percentages falling through the afternoon, 8, 7, 6, and of how he had blamed the wind, the cold, the bent rim.

He went outside in his jacket with a torch and stood at the free-throw line. The backyard was silent except for something small moving under the hedge. He took one shot, cold, no warm-up, and missed it badly, and then he laughed once, quietly, at the small perfect demonstration of everything he had just written down. He took the ball inside, washed his hands, and set the tablet to dim.

On Sunday he showed Ms. Nikolaidis the program. She read it slowly, and he watched her finger stop on the Saturday row, the box, the word. "Rest," she said.

"Ten hours in bed," Samuel said. "That's the aim. That's what the players did."

She looked at him a long moment, and he could not tell whether she was assessing the program or the shadows under his eyes, whether she had already worked out how he had spent his nights. "Tryouts are Friday," she said. "Start tonight."

He walked home across the frost-stiff grass and put the graph paper on his desk, the columns still neat, the warm-ups still scheduled, and beside the program he set his phone, face down, with the alarm set for a time he had never once used. Then he turned off the lamp and lay in the dark, listening to the house settle, wide awake.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Psychologist Robert Zajonc's 1968 experiments showed the mere-exposure effect: people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often.
story:
The last box took forty minutes to load because Emily insisted the trunk follow a logic only she could see: books with books, the record player wedged where it couldn't shift, the crate of chemistry notes flat on its back like a patient. Hajar had sat on the porch steps through all of it, narrating. "Now she's protecting the notes. Emily, you're going to a town with a science program, why are you hauling your old ones?" Sylas had said the notes were evidence, in case anyone at the new school accused her of not being smart, and then he had to apologize to her mother for the word "accused," which made no sense, which was the point.

Now the porch was behind them, and the town, and then the water tower with the faded cougar on it, which had been ugly for as long as Emily could remember and which she watched in the side mirror until it folded behind a hill. She held the farewell gift Hajar had pressed into her hands at the last second, wrapped in a paper bag from the pharmacy: a battered paperback called Forty Things Psychology Taught Us, secondhand, three dollars penciled inside the cover. "You're going to be insufferable at parties with this," Hajar had said. "I'm giving you material."

Her father drove with the calm of a man performing a fiduciary duty, which was in fact what he called the drive, since the car held everything the family owned that mattered and he'd refused to let anyone else take a turn at the wheel. Her mother read aloud from a printed sheet of facts about the new town, mispronouncing the main street's name twice, then a third time on purpose to make Emily laugh, which worked even though Emily had decided on principle not to laugh for the whole first hour.

She opened the book somewhere in the middle, out of spite, skipping Hajar's penciled suggestions in the margins. Item nineteen: in 1968, a psychologist named Robert Zajonc ran experiments showing the mere-exposure effect, that people tend to like things more simply because they have seen them more often. She read it twice. "Did you know," she said to the back seat in general, "that the more you see something, the more you like it? This guy Zajonc proved it in 1968. It's called the mere-exposure effect." Her mother said "mm" in the tone she used for facts she intended to forget. Her father said, "That's how billboards work," with a driver's certainty, and Emily said maybe, but it wasn't just advertising, it was faces, music, whole streets.

She tested it against her own history, quietly, while the fields ran out and the hills started. She had hated Sylas for the first six weeks of tenth grade, before they were assigned adjacent lab stations and his face became familiar and then necessary. She had hated the bus route she'd ridden since she was twelve, hated it with a specific private hatred, and could not actually remember when the hatred had dissolved into something so comfortable she could fall asleep on it. "So the trick," she said, mostly to herself, "is that you can't choose. The liking just arrives. You see it enough and it grows on you like mold."

Her mother twisted around in her seat. "You're saying you'll like the new town whether you want to or not?" Emily considered. It was tempting to believe the effect worked like a tide, patient and guaranteed, but that felt like the kind of comfort a person reaches for on purpose, which the book hadn't promised. Maybe the effect applied to the new town's bus route, its grocery store, its particular shade of streetlight, and not to the missing part, the part with names. Maybe she could compartmentalize it that way: let the exposure do its slow work on surfaces, and keep Hajar's and Sylas's absence in a separate drawer, unlabeled. Or maybe that was cowardice dressed up as strategy. She honestly could not tell yet, and said so, and her mother said, "Good, an honest scientist," and turned back around.

The phone buzzed against her leg. Sylas, obviously; he had claimed the job of texting her every landmark she lost, and had just sent a photograph of the pharmacy where Hajar worked, captioned "your gift's birthplace, now indigent without your business." Hajar replied beneath him a minute later: "ignore him. also ignore chapter 8, it's about rats." Emily typed "the rat chapter is the best one," then looked up and realized the hills had gotten serious, gold and stacked, and that she had no memory of the last twenty miles of them, and that this was probably fine.

There was a rest stop ahead, and her father signaled early, the way he did when he'd decided something was good for all of them. In the parking lot, squinting in the flat afternoon light, she took a photograph of the hills, of nothing in them, and sent it to the group chat with the caption "exposure begins now." Sylas answered within seconds: "we'll see if it grows on you." Hajar sent back only a small green check mark, which between the three of them had always meant the same thing, and Emily put the phone face-down on her knee and went to help her mother find the granola bars.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1, the usual North American graduation processional, premiered in 1901 in Liverpool.
story:
The folding chairs had been arranged in rows so exact they looked sedimentary, layer upon layer of graduating seniors pressed into the gymnasium floor, and Adam had been assigned a seat between a girl he'd never spoken to and a boy who had once thrown a lacrosse ball at his head in ninth grade. That was what alphabetical order did to people. It didn't care that he and Beatrice and Harley had been a unit since sophomore year, or that Harley was currently sitting four rows ahead, turning around in his chair with the persistence of a groundhog checking for spring.

They had been funnelled into the corridor outside the double doors to wait, because the processional could not begin until the parents were all seated and the parents were never all seated on time. Somewhere behind Adam, a tuba player in the concert band was quietly warming up, and then someone began to hum the tune the trumpets would soon carry, that slow looping melody that everyone in North America knew without being able to name. Adam hummed it too, and then, because the corridor was hot and there was nothing else to do, he wondered aloud where it had actually come from.

"It's called Pomp and Circumstance," said the tuba player, whose name was not on Adam's list of problems. "March Number One. Elgar wrote it." He said this in the tone of a person who had once been corrected on the subject and never recovered.

Adam took out his phone, which was technically forbidden, and searched it. Liverpool, he read. It premiered in Liverpool in 1901. He said this to Beatrice, who stood beside him holding her cap the way a person holds a hat they intend to throw. "So every graduation in the country," she said, "is walking to a piece of music that premiered in Liverpool in 1901, and nobody knows that." Adam said that his mother had walked to it, and probably her mother, and that the tune had been played at him so many times in movies and television that it had probably desensitized him completely, so that he could hear it now without feeling anything except the faint obligation to feel something. "That's a low bar," Beatrice said. "Most of today is a low bar."

The actual problem, the one Adam had been carrying around for two weeks, was that Beatrice was leaving for Montreal in August and he had not said anything about it, and there were now perhaps ninety minutes left in which saying something was convenient, after which saying it would require intention, and intention was not his strongest suit. Harley, naturally, had opinions. Harley had opinions on everything, including the temperature of the corridor, which he voiced over his shoulder at intervals.

"Tell her before we walk in," Harley said, when Adam drifted up the row under cover of adjusting his gown. "That way if it goes badly you only have to sit near her for one hour, and the music will drown out any crying."

"That's an indictment of your whole theory of relationships," Adam said, though privately he recognized the logic. Harley's theory of relationships was that they were best conducted at moments when an exit already existed, a fire door, a bell schedule, a graduation. It was a coward's theory and it had worked for Harley for four years.

Adam's own theory, to the extent he had one, was the opposite and no better: that important things should be said with no exit available, at a dinner table, in a parked car, so that the words had to be lived with. Both theories assumed the saying was the hard part. Neither accounted for the possibility that the saying was easy and the living was hard, which he suspected was the actual arrangement.

The doors opened. The trumpets picked up the Liverpool melody and the sedimentary rows began to dissolve from the front, the band teacher conducting with a small economical motion, as if the whole thing were already over and she were just tidying up. The girl beside Adam stood, and the boy who had thrown the lacrosse ball stood, and the line moved through the doors into air that smelled of floor wax and perfume and a gymnasium full of overdressed relatives, all of them raising their phones at once, a field of small lights.

Adam walked. He found Beatrice's mortarboard ahead of him in the line, a dark plank of heads with hers somewhere among them, and he kept his eyes on it the way you keep your eyes on a shore. He had the fact in his head, Liverpool, 1901, Elgar, a tune a hundred and twenty years old being used again tonight for purposes its composer could not have imagined, and it seemed to him briefly that this was how most things worked, old materials, new arrangements, nobody fully consulted. He sat down in his assigned chair between strangers. Somewhere in the row ahead, Beatrice turned around once, found him, and looked at him a second longer than the occasion required. Adam put his hand in his pocket, where the folded note had been all morning, and moved his thumb along its edge, back and forth, while the principal stepped forward and said, "Parents, families, and friends."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The restaurant had put six of them at a table meant for four, and Kaylee's mother kept rearranging the bread basket as though it were the seating chart that needed fixing. Across from Kaylee, her father sat with his sleeves rolled up, the way he used to look on Sunday mornings before the split, and Lyric was telling a story about the graduation ceremony that Kaylee could tell was half invented, because Lyric invented things the way other people breathed.

"And then the principal said, diplomas will be conferred," Lyric said, "as if anyone knows what conferred means."

"I do," said Alma, who had driven two hours to be here and kept checking her phone under the table. "It means handed over with ceremony. Like a bribe, but legal."

Kaylee's mother laughed too loudly at that, and her father didn't, and the space between the two laughs was the whole shape of the last three years. Kaylee turned her water glass a quarter turn, then another quarter, until the condensation made a slow ring on the cloth.

She had the diploma folder in the canvas bag under her chair. She hadn't opened it yet. In the gym that afternoon, the principal had warned them not to open the folders on stage, some old superstition or maybe just crowd control, and she had carried it unopened through the photographs on the field, through the parking lot, through her grandmother's hug that smelled like rosewater and cigarettes. Now, between the appetizers and the mains, she lifted it out.

"Okay," she said. "Moment of truth."

The folder was burgundy leatherette with the school's crest stamped in gold, and it opened like a book. Inside, on a single flat sheet, her name in script, the date, a signature that was supposedly the principal's but looked photocopied. She held it up so the table could see.

"It's not even folded," Lyric said, leaning in. "After all that, it's just lying there."

"That's the joke, though," Kaylee said slowly, because something was assembling itself in her mind, half remembered from Mr. Hamdan's class, from the Tuesday he'd gone off script. "The word diploma. It comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double. They used to fold official documents, that's where it comes from. So this thing is named after a fold it doesn't have." She ran her thumb along the flat edge of the sheet. "It's a diploma that never got folded."

"A crease with commitment issues," Alma said, and the table laughed, even her father, and Kaylee found she was pleased in a way she couldn't quite locate, the way you're pleased when a door you thought was stuck turns out to open.

Later, when the mains had come and her parents were arguing in the low, careful voices they reserved for restaurants, about whether the turnpike or the parkway was faster to the aunt's house, Kaylee found herself watching Mr. Hamdan's text arrive: Congrats. You argued better than most of my seniors this year. Don't let college cure you of it. He had been the one who made them read the ethics unit twice, once for the arguments and once for the flaws in the arguments, and he had refused, absolutely refused, to tell them what he believed about any of it. When Lyric had accused him of relativism, of pretending nothing was true, he had said no, the difference between holding a view and pretending to hold one is the whole difference, and Kaylee had written it in the margin of her notebook and thought about it roughly every week since.

She thought about it now, over the pasta she wasn't tasting. Her father wanted her to take the scholarship to the state school, close, sensible, dinner on Sundays. Her mother wanted her to go far, wanted it so visibly that Kaylee suspected the wanting had more to do with her mother's own unfinished map than with Kaylee's. Both of them loved her; that much was not uncertain. Which choice was right was a different question, and the honest answer was that she could argue either side and mean neither, or mean both, and she didn't yet know whether that was weakness or just accuracy. Mr. Hamdan would say that not knowing, stated plainly, was itself a position, and she suspected he'd also say that a position you never commit to is a way of hiding. She suspected both of those things were true at once, which was exactly the kind of sentence that used to make Lyric throw popcorn at her.

"Earth to Kaylee," Lyric said. "Toast. You have to give a toast, it's the law."

Kaylee stood, glass of water raised, aware of her grandmother's camera coming up. "I was going to say something about the future," she said. "But the future's a big word and I just spent four years learning what happens to people who use big words without checking them." She looked down at the folder, still open beside her plate, the paper stubbornly flat. "So instead: to the fold we haven't made yet."

Her father's eyes did something complicated. Her mother reached over and closed the folder, gently, with one hand, as though finishing a sentence for her.

On the walk out, the evening had that diurnal collapse of June, the light going gold then gray in the space of a few minutes, and the air, still warm, seemed to invigorate even the strip-mall parking lot. Alma was leaving first, hugging everyone twice. Lyric was talking about the after-party. Kaylee stood by her mother's car holding the folder and, on an impulse she couldn't have defended, folded the diploma in half, the crease sharp under her thumbnail, then opened it again and looked at the line the fold had left.

"There," she said. "Now it's telling the truth."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
The mortgage papers were spread across his grandfather's kitchen table like a hand of cards neither player wanted to show. Two offers, one from the bank in town and one that had come in the mail, and at the top of each, in bold print, the interest rate. Grayson's grandfather tapped the higher number with one thick finger. "Five and a half percent," he said. "The fellow on the phone says that's good. I remember when it wasn't."

Grayson had driven out that morning with the excuse of helping carry boxes from the attic, but the boxes had become this: a rate lock that expired Friday, a bank officer who kept using the phrase "in this environment," and a grandfather who distrusted anything that arrived preapproved. "You're good with numbers," the old man said. It wasn't quite a compliment. It was closer to a plea.

He called Sameer from the back porch, phone pressed to one ear, the other filled with wind moving through the corn behind the fence. Sameer was the one who read econ blogs between classes and had opinions about everything except what to eat. "It's the Fed," Sameer said. "The Federal Reserve. They started raising the policy rate from basically zero in March of 2022, and they kept going until July of 2023, when it hit that range, 5.25 to 5.50 percent. That's the whole story of your grandfather's mortgage offer. That's why it's so different from a few years ago." Grayson wrote the numbers on the back of an envelope. "But why does raising it slow inflation?" he asked. Sameer's answer came back noncommittal, something about it being complicated, something about demand, and then the call dropped in the dead zone past the grain bins.

Inside, his grandfather was on the phone with the bank again, and Grayson sat across the table from the older of the two offers and tried to think. His grandfather wanted a smaller payment, wanted it badly enough to have cut the grass early and dressed in the good shirt for the banker's visit, badly enough that the roof estimate was folded into the same folder, waiting. Grayson wanted something smaller: to be the grandson who knew things, to earn the finger tapped against the number.

He thought about Grady, of all people. Grady had worked the summer at the hardware store and complained endlessly about customers who put purchases on store credit, then stopped buying when the interest on the store card jumped. Buying slows down when borrowing costs more. That was one half of it, the street-level half. Sameer had supplied the other half, the aerial view: the whole economy as one enormous store with one enormous card. Put the two together and something like a picture formed, though the seams still showed when he pressed on them. Why prices themselves had to fall in response, rather than just wages or jobs, he could not have said with any confidence, and he decided not to pretend otherwise.

When his grandfather hung up, Grayson pulled his chair around to the same side of the table. "Here's what I've got," he said. "The Federal Reserve is the central bank. When they raise the interest rate they control, borrowing gets expensive everywhere. Loans cost more, so people take fewer of them, so people buy less, so sellers can't keep pushing prices up. That's how raising rates slows inflation. And your five and a half percent, that's not the bank being greedy. The Fed pushed its rate up from near zero starting in March 2022 and didn't stop until it got to between 5.25 and 5.50 percent in July of 2023. Your offer is downstream of all that."

His grandfather looked at him for a long moment, and Grayson braced to be corrected. "Near zero," the old man repeated instead. "You're telling me money was practically free and now it isn't." He turned the offer over, reading it again with new suspicion, as though the page itself had been exonerated and something larger had taken its place on trial. "So I should take this one."

"I didn't say that," Grayson said. "I said why it looks the way it looks. Whether you lock it by Friday, that depends on the roof and on whether you could live with the payment if things got worse." It was a taxonomy of questions he was building in his head, he realized: what a thing is, why a thing is, and whether the thing is good for you. Three separate questions, and the banker kept smearing them into one.

His grandfather stood, tucked the folder under his arm, and said he was going to walk the fence line and think before the bank closed at five. At the gate he paused, and Grayson watched him look back toward the roof, then down the road toward town, then he took out his phone and dialed the bank's number right there in the field, waving for Grayson to bring the papers.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution: A History, published in 1837, stressed the moral choices of individuals rather than impersonal historical forces.
story:
Chase had promised himself he would start the historiography essay on Friday, and now it was Sunday evening and the prompt sat open on his laptop like an accusation: explain how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800, eight hundred words, due at eight in the morning. Ms. Qureshi had warned them against a timeline of names. "Historians disagree," she had said, tapping the whiteboard. "Your job is to show the disagreement, then take a side, or admit you can't." Chase had three browser tabs open, a PDF of a Marxist historian, a summary of a revisionist one, and a page of half-finished notes that read, in his own handwriting, "forces vs. people???"

He went down to the basement to look for the spare charger, which his mother insisted lived somewhere near the boxes of his grandfather's books, and there, in a box marked PAPERBACKS, he found a fat brown volume with a cracked spine: Thomas Carlyle, The French Revolution: A History. He carried it upstairs, blew dust off the cover, and checked the publication date twice. 1837. His grandfather had died before Chase started high school, and the discovery felt like a message, though he knew it was only a box.

The prose was not what he expected. Carlyle wrote like a thunderstorm, whole pages about Danton's face and Mirabeau's voice, about men choosing or failing to choose, and almost nothing about economics, grain prices, class structure, any of the machinery Chase had been told the modern historians cared about. Charlotte texted him a photo of her outline, color-coded, six tidy paragraphs, and he texted back a photo of the Carlyle instead. "What is that," she wrote. "Grandpa's book," he typed. "It's from 1837 and it stresses the moral choices of individuals instead of impersonal historical forces." "You're quoting the introduction," she said, and then, "Some of us have outlines." He put the phone face down.

Sierra called at nine, the way she did when she was avoiding her own homework. "Ms. Qureshi's going to want more than Carlyle," she said. "The whole point of historiography is that people changed their minds." Chase balanced the phone against the salt shaker and tried to explain: the Marxist he'd read treated the Revolution as a structural event, something that had to happen the way a river has to flow downhill, and Carlyle treated it as a drama in which everything depended on whether particular men behaved decently. "So which one is right?" Sierra asked. "That's the essay," Chase said. "That is a terrible answer," Sierra said, and hung up because her tea was boiling over.

He wrote half a paragraph and deleted it, then wrote it again. The problem was that both accounts could subsume the same events; the storming of the Bastille fit Carlyle's version and the structural version equally well, depending on which detail you looked at, and Chase did not yet know how to choose. He thought of the unit on existentialism from philosophy club, the idea that people are defined by their choices, and wondered briefly if Carlyle had simply been an early version of that, then felt guilty for the anachronism, though nobody would know.

It was nearly eleven when he found the note. A yellowed index card had been tucked between pages 400 and 401, in handwriting he recognized from birthday cards: his grandfather's. "For the paper," it said. "Don't be intransigent. Carlyle believed in heroes and villains. History might not. But look what he makes you feel." Chase sat very still. His grandfather had written a paper, or started one, on this same subject, with this same book, and had left the card here as if for a future reader who would never arrive, except that he had.

Chase texted Charlotte instead of Sierra this time, because Charlotte was the one who argued about evidence. "I found something in the book," he wrote, and sent a picture of the card. She replied with three exclamation points, then, "Are you going to say he was wrong?" Chase typed yes, then deleted it, then typed no, then deleted that too. The truth was stranger: Carlyle's account was overwhelming, the most alive thing Chase had read all month, and it stressed moral choices of individuals over impersonal forces so completely that it felt less like history than like a sermon, and yet the structural historians, dry as toast, had explanations Carlyle could not answer. He did not know how to hold both. That, he realized, was not a failure of the essay. That was the essay.

He wrote until one in the morning, and at 12:52 the last sentence he typed was about what remained uncertain, and he let it stand. Then he took the index card and slid it back between pages 400 and 401, exactly where his grandfather had left it, and closed the book, and carried it not down to the basement but up to his room, where he set it on the desk beside the laptop, spine facing out. "You too," he said, and turned off the lamp.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: Denmark, Norway and Sweden have no statutory national minimum wage; pay floors are instead set through collective agreements between unions and employers.
story:
The kitchen of the Copper Kettle ran on a rhythm Avery had learned before she'd learned to drive: the hiss of the flat-top when the cook dropped onions, the bell over the pass, the ticket printer chattering like something wounded. She had been bussing and prepping there for fourteen months, three nights a week and double shifts on Saturdays, saving for the deposit on a dorm room she'd seen exactly once, in a photograph. Tonight her paycheque sat folded in her back pocket, and folded inside it, a note she'd written herself: ask about the raise.

She asked during the lull between dinner and the bar crowd, when Mr. Baptiste came to the lowboy fridge for cream. He was the sous chef, broad-shouldered, mercurial in a way that kept everyone guessing whether his mood would swing toward jokes or thrown towels. "You've been here over a year," Avery said, keeping her voice level the way her mother had taught her for talking to landlords. "Training the new bussers. I was wondering about a raise, and the scheduling thing, closing three nights in a row."

Mr. Baptiste didn't laugh, which surprised her. He glanced toward the office door at the back of the kitchen, where the owner counted receipts behind fogged glass. "There's a meeting Sunday," he said quietly. "Staff only. Back room of Alina's aunt's hall. You want the raise, you come to the meeting first." Then he carried the cream away as if he'd said nothing, and the printer spat out another ticket, and Avery stood with her hands in the sanitizer water, wondering what she'd just agreed to.

She had context for it, sort of. In her economics class that week, the students had been split into teams to debate raising the minimum wage, and she'd drawn the negative side, which she didn't believe, which was apparently the point. Greyson, on her team, had been captivated by a statistic about small-business closures and kept repeating it until Alina, from across the room, told him the number was from a blog. What Avery remembered most was the moment their teacher asked whether every wealthy country had a legal minimum wage, and Alina said yes, obviously, and the teacher said no, and let the silence sit there like a challenge nobody picked up. It had bothered Avery for two days, the way an unfinished crossword bothers her, so that Friday night she'd looked it up on her phone in the break room between the salad station and the dish pit.

What she found had rearranged something in her head. Denmark, Norway and Sweden had no statutory national minimum wage at all. Not a low one, not a complicated one; none. Instead, pay floors came out of collective agreements, bargained between unions and employers, sector by sector. She read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to contradict everything the debate had assumed. She'd been arguing, with false conviction, that without a legal floor workers would be paid nothing, and here were countries full of workers being paid well, apparently, without one. She screenshotted the page and texted it to Greyson with no comment, and he replied only with a question mark.

Sunday, the back room of the hall smelled of coffee and folding chairs. Nine of them: two servers, the line cook named Deshawn, the dishwasher, Alina's aunt's friend who did banquets, and Avery, youngest by six years. A woman from the union local stood at the front with a corkboard, and she didn't lecture. She asked them what they wanted and wrote it on index cards and pinned it up: wage scales posted where everyone could see them, notice before schedule changes, premium pay for closes, a grievance procedure so nobody could be fired on a bad night's whim. "This is what collective bargaining is," she said, tapping the corkboard. "You decide together what you need, and you negotiate for it together."

Avery kept thinking about the Scandinavian thing while the woman talked. She raised her hand, feeling like she was still in class. "I read that Denmark and Norway and Sweden don't have a national minimum wage in law," she said. "The pay floors come from collective agreements between the unions and the employers." The woman nodded. "That's right." Avery sat with that for a second. "So the floor exists either way," she said slowly. "It's just that in some places the law is the floor, and in others, the agreement is." She wasn't sure which she trusted more, and she said so, and the dishwasher, a quiet man named only Tomás in her mind, said in accented English, "The law doesn't know my boss. The agreement, he signs it."

The vote to proceed was held by secret ballot, torn strips of paper into an empty coffee tin, and Avery's strip said yes, though her hand had hovered over the pen longer than she expected. She wanted the raise; that part was simple. What was less simple was knowing that if the owner felt cornered, he could close early on weeknights, cut hours to skeleton shifts, let the slow season do his dirty work. The woman from the local had named that possibility herself, hadn't hidden it, and Avery respected her for it and feared it a little.

Monday, Mr. Baptiste found her at the prep station and set a container of tarragon down beside her cutting board. "I put your name forward to be on the committee," he said. "Three of us, meeting the owner Thursday. You'll speak for the back of house." Avery's first instinct was to say she was seventeen, but she stopped herself, because the number hadn't stopped him. "What do I say about the raise?" she asked. He shrugged, already turning back toward the line. "What you told me. You've been here a year. You train the new ones. Say the rest yourself." The flat-top hissed, the bell rang over the pass, and the printer began its chattering again.

Thursday she wore the one blouse that wasn't stained and walked into the office with the corkboard cards copied in her own handwriting. The owner sat behind the fogged glass with his accountant's fiduciary caution spread across his face, and before he could open his mouth, Avery set her pages on the desk between them and slid them forward. "These are the floor," she said. "Let's start there."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
The tour guide stopped them under a copper beech whose roots had buckled the pavement into a low ridge, and Ryan, standing at the back, kept one foot on either side of the ridge as though straddling a border. The campus was three hours from home by train, and his application to its engineering program had been sitting in some admissions office for eleven days. He had begun counting the days without deciding to, the way you begin counting the days since someone died.

"Most of you are juniors," the guide said, "so you're just starting to look. Seniors, you already know the waiting game." A few people laughed. Ryan did not. Beside him, a girl with a lanyard twisted around her finger was frowning at her phone.

"Sorry," she said, catching him noticing. "It's just my list. I keep rewriting it." She held the screen out as if it were evidence. "I'm applying in England, through UCAS, and you can only choose five courses. Five. And then the list goes in with no order of preference, so the universities can't even tell which one you actually want. They all just see five names, all equal." Her name was Juliane, he learned later, when the guide asked them to say names and hometowns in a circle that nobody formed properly.

"That's a strange system," Ryan said.

"It's efficient. One application, five choices, and no ranked order, so nobody's penalized for aiming high and hedging low at the same time." She scrolled again. "The problem is the choosing. I've got it down to eight and I can't kill three of them."

Ryan thought of his own application, single and singular, one program at one school, submitted early against the advice of his father, who had said that applying early decision was like proposing before the first date. Ryan had done it anyway because the program was good and because, in October, certainty had felt like a virtue. In February, certainty felt like a room with one door.

There had been a night in the autumn, before the deadline, when his father sat across the kitchen table with the application open on the laptop between them. "You're seventeen," his father had said. "You're allowed to keep your options vague." Ryan had tapped the submit button just to preempt the argument, and remembered, afterward, the small blue confirmation screen and the strange flatness of getting what he wanted. That flatness had not left. It surfaced whenever someone asked where he was going to college and he heard himself say the name too quickly, preempting the next question, which was always, and if you don't get in?

The tour moved on toward the engineering building, a concrete slab softened by ivy that some committee was evidently too sentimental to remove. Juliane fell into step beside him. "What about you?" she asked. "How many did you apply to?"

"One," Ryan said. "One program, one school." He heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Everyone said diversify. My friend Zavier applied to nine schools and he's got a spreadsheet with columns for financial aid and weather and distance from a Chipotle. He calls it his portfolio. He thinks I'm reckless."

"Are you?"

"I thought certainty was the mature thing. Now I think maybe certainty is just a decision you made before you had enough information, and then you defend it because undoing it costs more than keeping it." He looked at the ivy, its small dark leaves aslant on the wind. "My physiology teacher, Ms. Fraser, told us once that the body keeps its options open. Redundant systems, she called them. Two kidneys. Two lungs. You survive the failure of one because you never committed everything to a single organ."

"Ms. Fraser sounds like she'd approve of UCAS."

"She'd approve of five courses, no preference order, all equal in the eyes of the universities." He smiled. "Though she'd also say the liver is nonredundant, so at some point everything commits."

Inside the engineering building, an undergraduate was demonstrating a robotic arm to a cluster of parents, and the arm was misbehaving, its wrist rotating past its target again and again in a stubborn, exact overshoot. "The calibration's gone recalcitrant," the student said, half to the machine, half to the room, and smacked the housing once with the flat of his hand. The arm corrected itself, gripped the block, and set it down with terrible precision. Ryan watched it and thought about overshoot, about how he had aimed at this school so hard that the aiming had become the whole project, distinct from wanting.

"So kill three," he said to Juliane, as the group drifted toward the exit.

"That's the instruction, yes. Thank you, very helpful." But she was looking at her list again. "Two of them are places I've never visited. One of them is somewhere my mother wants me to go. One is somewhere I decided I wanted when I was fourteen and I'm not sure the reasons survived."

"Then maybe those are your three. The one you've never seen, the one that isn't yours, and the one that belonged to a fourteen-year-old." He heard himself give this advice and recognized, with some discomfort, that it was also an instruction he would not take himself, since his own list had one item on it and that item was all of those things at once.

Juliane typed something, deleted it, typed again. "Five," she said. "No order of preference. God, it's like being asked to shuffle your own future and pretend the shuffle means nothing." She pocketed the phone. "If you get in, will you actually go? Honestly."

Outside, the beech tree stood where they had left it, roots still ridging the pavement, and Ryan put his foot on the ridge again before he answered. "I don't know," he said. "Ask me in April."

He took out his phone and, instead of checking his email as he had done at every corner of the tour, opened the browser and typed, in the search bar, universities still accepting applications.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: After a concussion, athletes return through graduated steps from rest to full play, moving to the next step only while they stay free of symptoms.
story:
The rink at six in the morning had a smell Xavier thought of as igneous, like the building itself had cooled from something molten into this hard white plain. He was the first one on the ice for the optional skate, because playoffs started Friday and because Coach had told them, twice, that the lineup would be posted Thursday night. He took the puck along the boards, wristed it into the empty net, and did it again until his ankles burned.

Lilah arrived halfway through, still in her street shoes, carrying her helmet instead of wearing it. She had been out for three weeks since the hit behind the net in the Riverside game, and everyone knew she was dying to come back, though nobody said it that plainly to her face. She sat on the bench and laced her skates with the concentration of someone defusing something.

"How'd it go with the trainer?" Xavier asked, drifting over to the boards.

"I'm on the next step. Light drills with the team, no contact." She snapped her chin strap. "If I stay fine through today and tomorrow, I can practice fully Thursday, and then Friday." She said it like a recipe she'd memorized, which in a way it was. The trainer had given her the whole ladder after her concussion: you start at rest, and you only move up to the next step if you get through the current one without symptoms. Any symptom, and you drop back a stage and start the climb over. Six steps between her couch and Friday's opening faceoff, and today was step four.

Gregory showed up at seven with two breakfast sandwiches and the general air of an epicure at a bad buffet, complaining that the arena café had stopped selling the good ones. He was the one who told Xavier, quietly, on the bench during a water break, "She looked off in the passing drill. Kept rubbing her temple."

Xavier watched her instead of the puck for the rest of the hour. There it was, once: a pass she'd have taken in stride a month ago, and instead she hesitated, blinked, pressed the heel of her hand to her forehead for half a second before resuming. Everyone else was watching the puck. Nobody else was watching her.

He caught her in the hallway by the skate sharpening booth, where the grinding noise gave them a little privacy. "Your head," he said. Not a question.

"I'm fine. It's just tired. I didn't sleep."

"You rubbed your temple twice during the drill."

She stared at him with the particular fury of someone who knows she's caught. "Do you understand what happens if I say it out loud? I go back down a step. Today was light drills, and if I'm symptomatic I don't move up tomorrow, I move back, and then Thursday isn't full practice, and Friday I'm not on the roster. Friday is playoffs. Do you get that? I have one shot at a playoff game in my whole life and it's this one."

Xavier had spent two years envying the way she played, the fearlessness of it, and had spent the last three weeks thinking about the trainer's laminated sheet that she'd once shown him in the cafeteria. For a while he'd thought the steps were bureaucratic, an insult to a competitor's judgment: you know your own body, you know when you're ready. But the opposite idea had been ionizing something in him since the morning he'd watched her blink at that pass, a slow charged change in how he saw the whole thing. The steps weren't there because they doubted her courage. They were there because a person in the middle of wanting something this badly was the least reliable witness to her own symptoms. He knew that now from the inside, because part of him wanted to say nothing and let her play.

"The trainer's still in the office until eight," he said.

"If I go back down a stage, Friday's gone."

"If you play Friday with a headache nobody knows about and take a hit, everything's gone. Not just the game." He heard how it sounded, like a line from a poster, and hated it, and kept going anyway, quieter. "I'll walk over with you. You don't have to make it sound like a big deal. You just say it started during light drills."

She looked through the glass at the empty ice, where the zam had just finished and the surface was pure and unmarked, and for a long moment neither of them moved. Then she unclipped her helmet and held it against her hip.

"Fine," she said. "But you're telling Gregory he's taking my spot on the power play. He's been insufferable about those sandwiches all week."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
knowledge_domain: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
fact: In Bastiat's broken-window parable, money spent replacing a window could otherwise have bought shoes or a book, so the breakage creates no net gain.
story:
The acceptance letter had been on the fridge for eleven days, held up by a magnet shaped like a lobster, and Marcus had stopped seeing it. What he saw instead, every night, was his father doing the math out loud. Tuition, residence, the meal plan he called "the expensive one" and his mother called "the only one." Tonight the math had a new variable: Mr. Leung, who owned the hardware store two streets over, had offered Marcus the summer inventory job at forty hours a week. His father was enthusiastic in the quiet way that made refusal feel like a diplomatic incident.

Malek had come for dinner because his own kitchen was being renovated, a fact he narrated with pride, as though the torn-up floor were an achievement. "Honestly, the flood was the best thing that happened to us," he said, reaching for the rice. "The pipe bursts, the contractor gets a huge job, my uncle's cousin does the tiling, everybody's working. My dad says it stimulated the whole street."

"Money's not free, though," Marcus said. It came out before he'd fully decided to say it, the way things did at the table, where his father's attention was a searchlight that swept past at intervals.

"What's that supposed to mean?"

"The money your dad paid the contractor," Marcus said. "He was saving it for something. The trip to Turkey, I think he mentioned it. So the flood didn't create anything. It just moved the money from the plane tickets to the tile."

Malek chewed on this, and on the chicken. "The tiler got paid, though."

"The tiler got paid and the airline didn't. If the pipe hadn't burst, your dad would have the trip and the tiler would have somebody else's bathroom." Marcus had read the parable three weeks ago, in a battered economics paperback Mr. Leung kept by the register for slow afternoons, and he hadn't known until this moment that he'd actually absorbed it. A boy breaks a window; the glazier profits; the town calls it good business. But the money spent replacing the window could have bought shoes or a book, so the breakage creates no net gain. Broken window, tile floor, same arithmetic. He was a little stunned by how neatly it had surfaced, like a fish rising.

"Turkey in October is cheaper anyway," Malek said, which was not agreement but had the shape of it.

His father, however, had gone very still, in the manner of a man recalibrating his argument. "Interesting," he said. "Because by that logic, if you take the inventory job, the money you earn comes from somewhere."

"From Mr. Leung. He pays me for work he actually needs done. Nobody's breaking anything."

"You know what you'd be giving up." His father said it lightly, the way you'd mention weather. Jeremie had texted Marcus that afternoon, twice: the road trip was firming up, two weeks in August, a borrowed van, a lake nobody had named yet. Marcus had not replied. The trip cost almost nothing and cost everything: forty hours a week at the store left no window for it, and August was the whole of what remained before everything began.

His mother said the green beans were getting cold, which in her language meant the conversation was.

"Jeremie's counting on me," Marcus said. "He needs a second driver. The van's insured for two."

"Jeremie," his father said, "found out about the trip on Tuesday and has been counting on you since approximately Tuesday." This was accurate, and Marcus resented how accurate it was, because it meant his father had been thinking about Jeremie, had been mapping the whole terrain of the decision while Marcus was still standing at its edge calling it a view.

"I'm not saying the job's a punishment," Marcus said. "I get that it's the smart money. I'm saying the trip is worth something too, and it's not nothing, and I don't know how to make those two things sit in the same column."

His father put down his fork. For a moment Marcus thought a speech was coming, something about the real world, and braced for it the way he braced for his mother's opinion of the meal plan. Instead his father said, "When I was eighteen I turned down a trip to Spain. My friend Tomas went without me. He still talks about it. I never mention it, which you may have noticed is its own kind of mentioning."

"That's not an argument," Marcus said.

"It's not. It's inventory." His father picked up the fork again. "You like inventory. Take the weekend."

Malek, who had been silent through all of this in the manner of a guest watching a sport whose rules were unclear to him, said, "For what it's worth, my dad says October in Turkey is the best month."
