He helped himself to more rice, gratuitously, a third serving nobody had offered, and looked at Marcus with the expression of a boy who understood that the pipe had already burst somewhere and the only question was who got the tile.

Marcus took out his phone under the table and typed to Jeremie: not a yes, not a no. "Maybe the second week of August. Asking about shifts." Then he put it face down beside his plate and ate the cold green beans, because they were there, and because his mother was watching, and because for two more days the window was still unbroken either way.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Claude Monet painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year.
story:
On the first Monday of the art intensive at Camp Wren, Madeline pinned ten empty sheets of newsprint to the wall of the studio and wrote "THEME" at the top in pencil, then crossed it out, then wrote it again. Ms. Gupta had said the portfolio had to cohere, ten works plus a statement, and that cohesion was harder than skill. Madeline had assumed the opposite. She could already draw; what she couldn't do was decide what all of it was about.

She chose the lightning-split oak behind the canoe shed because it was close and because nobody else had claimed it. For four days she painted it at odd hours: once at six in the morning with the mist still lying in the grass, once at noon, once in the rain. On Thursday she stood in front of the three studies with Carys, who had a theme about her grandmother's hands and had already finished six pieces.

"Isn't it the same tree three times?" Carys said. She said it kindly, which was worse.

"It's different light," Madeline said. "That's the point."

"Is it a point, though, or an excuse?"

In the camp library that afternoon, a room that was really three shelves and a moth, Madeline looked for something to prove herself right. She found a fat paperback with a cracked spine, opened it sideways at random, and stopped. Claude Monet had painted more than thirty views of the facade of Rouen Cathedral in 1892 and 1893, showing it under different light at different times of day and year. More than thirty. She counted the plates in the book, then read the sentence again to make sure the years were the ones she thought. Thirty paintings of one building, and the building was the excuse and the light was the subject, or maybe the other way around; the book didn't fully commit, and neither, she noticed, did the paintings. The cathedral in morning light looked like butter; in the grey afternoon it looked like ash. Nothing about the stone had changed.

She carried the book to the dock, where Alessandro was skipping flat stones with the concentration of an acolyte performing a rite he only half believed in. She read the sentence aloud. He skipped a stone, watched it sink, and considered.

"So your tree is your cathedral," he said. "Very impressive. You've achieved being a dead French man."

"I'm saying repetition isn't laziness."

"I'm saying you'd better not hand in ten paintings of bark." He said it without looking at her, which was how he said things he meant.

That night she worked it out at the picnic table outside the mess hall, in the light of the bug zapper, with Ms. Gupta collecting cups two tables over. Madeline had been treating the theme like a label: tree, or light, or whatever would make the portfolio sound serious. But Monet hadn't picked a subject so much as picked a question, and the question was what stayed the same when everything visible changed. The stone stayed; the light didn't; the painting lived in the gap. She thought about her own three studies, how the morning one was quiet and honest and the noon one was florid, all exaggerated ochre, because she'd been showing off for an audience that didn't exist. She could sublimate that vanity into something useful, she supposed, if she was honest about which painting was lying.

The problem she couldn't solve was Carys's question, still sitting there under everything: was she asking a real question or decorating an easy one? She didn't know. Maybe ten paintings would answer it and maybe they'd just repeat it in different weather. She wrote that in her sketchbook, in the draft statement, because Ms. Gupta had said the statement could hold doubt as long as it held it openly: I don't yet know whether the tree changes or only my seeing of it.

On Saturday she got up at five without telling anyone, took the good paper and the travel kit, and walked out through the wet grass. The oak stood where she'd left it, split down the middle, half of it dead. She set up, mixed a grey she hadn't tried before, and began the fourth painting. Behind her the bug zapper clicked off; the cook's radio came on in the kitchen. She painted until her tea went cold, then stood back and looked at what she had.

"Still a tree," she said to nobody. She sat down again and picked up the brush.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food-safety guidance says refrigerated food must be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 degrees Fahrenheit) to slow the growth of bacteria.
story:
The food bank ran out of the animal shelter's basement, which struck Owen as strange until Mr. Islam explained that the shelter owned the building and rented the low floor to the pantry on winter mornings, when the dogs upstairs were too loud to adopt out anyway. Owen had signed up because his mother had mentioned it once, in passing, in October, and the mention had sat in him like a seed until he could not stand to let another Saturday go by unused. He wanted, though he would not have said it this way, to be the kind of person who showed up.

He arrived at eight and found the loading dock already busy. A man with a clipboard was waving a van into the alley, and a girl about Owen's age was hauling cardboard boxes toward the basement stairs. "You must be the new one," she said. "I'm Clara. Boxes go down the ramp, not the stairs. The ramp's slower but nobody dies." She said it without smiling, and Owen understood within ten minutes that this was simply her manner, brisk and complete, like a good set of instructions.

The third volunteer was Andrei, who had been coming for two years and who Mr. Islam, the pantry's coordinator, called "our institutional memory" with a straight face. Andrei knew where the lentils were kept, which families liked the brown rice and which pretended not to, and how many bags of carrots constituted a month's supply. He was taciturn in the mornings and loosened by noon, and he had opinions about everything, delivered flatly, as though reporting weather. "The dairy goes in the walk-in first," he told Owen, handing him a crate. "Always first. Milk waits for nobody."

Owen carried two crates down the ramp and then came back up for the third, which was when he saw it: four gallons of milk and a sleeve of yogurt containers, sitting on the dock's concrete lip, in the sun, beside a pallet of canned soup. The van that had delivered them had pulled away. The milk had clearly been there for a while; the plastic was warm on the side facing the light. He stood over it for a moment, doing the arithmetic of his own uncertainty. He knew the number because his mother had once left groceries in the car for an afternoon and had spent the evening anxious about it, reading aloud from her phone: refrigerated food had to be kept at or below 4 degrees Celsius, 40 degrees Fahrenheit, to slow the growth of bacteria. He had rolled his eyes at the time, seventeen and sure that his mother's caution was something a person could be inured to, like cold water. Now the number came back to him with unexpected weight.

He carried the milk down to the walk-in anyway, and then found Mr. Islam by the folding tables where the bags were assembled. "There was milk on the dock," Owen said. "In the sun. I put it in the cooler but it was already warm." Mr. Islam set down his tape gun. "How warm," he said, not as a question but as a demand, and Owen said the plastic was warm to the touch, the sun-facing side, maybe half an hour, maybe more, and Mr. Islam closed his eyes briefly, the way a man does when he has been waiting all morning for the thing he feared.

"You did right telling me," Mr. Islam said, and then he stood in the middle of the basement holding a gallon in each hand, and Owen watched a decision move through him. Andrei came over and put his hand on one of the gallons, then on the metal shelf of the walk-in, comparing. "Dump it," he said. "That's the rule. Four Celsius, forty Fahrenheit, that's the line, and these crossed it hours ago." Mr. Islam said, "Eight families take milk on Saturdays." Andrei said, "Eight families take milk, not eight families take their chances." Nobody spoke. Clara, stacking cans with her back to them, said, "There's a corner store two blocks over. I can run up a collection during the shift. It won't cover everything but it'll cover most."

Owen expected Mr. Islam to decide quickly, the way the adults in his life usually decided, but instead the man walked the length of the basement and back, still holding the milk, and Owen understood that the decision had costs on both sides that he, at eighteen, could see but not weigh. Throwing out food offended something in Mr. Islam that Owen recognized, a belief that waste was a kind of insult to the people who had donated it and the people who would have eaten it. Serving it offended something else, older and quieter.

In the end Mr. Islam carried the gallons to the sink himself and poured them out, slowly, and then stood there with the empty containers and said, to no one in particular, "Sixteen years I've done this and I've never once had to pour out milk." Clara was already out the door with a coffee can and a plan. Andrei went back to the lentils without comment, though at noon, loosened, he told Owen about a volunteer from years back, a retired chemist everyone had called the savant of spoilage, who could smell a bad yogurt through the lid. "Nobody ever checked the dock when he was here," Andrei said. "He'd stand out there like a foreman. Then he moved to Ottawa."

They served forty-one families that morning. Two went without milk, and one woman took the shelf-stable cartons Clara had scrounged and said they were fine, fine, though her tone suggested a ledger of small disappointments being quietly updated. Owen stayed to sweep, and Mr. Islam sat on the folding table watching him, and after a while he said, "Next week, when you come, check the dock first thing. Before the boxes. Before anything." It was not praise exactly, but Owen took it as something adjacent to trust. He wondered, sweeping, whether he would have told Mr. Islam if the milk had been the only thing donated all day, whether his own certainty would have held under that pressure, and he did not know, and he swept the thought into the pile with the dust and carried both out the back door and set them down in the sun.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: Under the 2017 American guideline, stage 1 hypertension means a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89.
story:
Ethan had never once fainted, which he told anyone who asked, and nobody had asked, so he told Mikaella anyway on Tuesday morning while she unpacked her laptop in the health sciences room. Mr. Nielsen had posted the assignment on the board: each student would take a real blood pressure log, interpret one reading, and explain in plain language how diet and exercise could change the numbers. Ethan had brought his grandfather's log, three weeks of morning readings copied in ballpoint onto graph paper, because his own log, kept for one day, contained a single entry and a doodle of a shark.

"Whose is that?" Mikaella asked, tilting her chin at the graph paper.

"Mine," Ethan said. Then, after a pause that he did not consider a pause, "It's my grandpa's. He lives with us. I copied it out."

Mikaella had known Ethan since tenth grade and had learned to accept that his sentences arrived in installments. She pulled up the guideline summary Mr. Nielsen had linked, a dense page of thresholds and stages that she scrolled through at a glacial pace while Ethan remonstrated with the trackpad, tapping it as though speed could be transferred through plastic. "Scroll," he said. "It's somewhere in the middle."

Marilou arrived with a paper cup of coffee and sat backwards on her chair. "I already found my part," she said. "My mom's log is boring, everything's like 118 over 74. I need something to actually say."

Ethan had something to say. He had noticed it the night before, at the kitchen table, when he had spread the log out and found that the last six readings had crept upward: 132 over 82, then 134 over 84, then 138 over 86. He had not mentioned this to anyone at home. His grandfather had a talent for waving off anything that smelled like a fuss, and Ethan's father had a complementary talent for starting fusses, and between the two of them the household had worked out an equilibrium that Ethan had no intention of disturbing. He was, he maintained, a calm person. His hands were steady. That the graph paper had a small tear in one corner, bent back and forth during that kitchen-table hour, was the paper's own business.

He found the line in the guideline summary. He read it twice, then a third time, moving his lips, and Marilou watched him do it.

"Stage one hypertension," Ethan said, reading aloud. "That's what they call it."

"Call what?"

He pointed at the screen. Under the 2017 American guideline, he saw, stage 1 hypertension meant a systolic reading of 130 to 139 or a diastolic reading of 80 to 89. He checked his grandfather's numbers against the ranges, column by column, and the last six readings sat inside them like coins in a slot.

"So he has it," Marilou said, looking over his shoulder. "Your grandpa."

"He has numbers," Ethan said. "Numbers aren't the same as having something."

Mikaella turned her laptop toward him. "It says he should probably see a doctor."

"It says that about everyone. The whole document is a morass of shoulds." He said this with more confidence than he felt, and he was aware of it, the way you are aware of a floor that creaks under a guest. The truth, which he set aside the way you set aside a plate you intend to wash later, was that his grandfather had not seen a doctor in two years and had announced at dinner in October that he intended to keep the streak. The readings were new. The monitor was new too, a gift from Ethan's aunt, and for the first week his grandfather had tested himself with the solemnity of a man proving he was fine. Ethan had watched him do it. He had not watched closely.

Mr. Nielsen came around the tables during the last twenty minutes, checking drafts. He stopped at Ethan's elbow and looked at the graph paper, then at the screen, and asked only what Ethan planned to argue. Ethan began with the part about diet, the part he had prepared, how the assignment wanted him to connect the numbers on the page to salt and walking and the rest of it, and he got through that part smoothly because it was abstract and involved no one's actual grandfather.

"And the reading itself?" Mr. Nielsen said. "What are you going to do about the reading itself?"

"I'm going to interpret it," Ethan said.

"Interpret it to whom?"

That was the question. Ethan had assumed, without examining the assumption, that the interpretation was for the grade, for Mr. Nielsen, for the rubric with its tidy columns. But a number written in his grandfather's ballpoint hand, sitting inside those published ranges, did not care about rubrics, and somewhere between the second and third reading of the guideline Ethan had understood that an interpretation that stayed inside a classroom was not an interpretation at all. It was a hiding place.

At the end of class Marilou slid her coffee cup across the table. "You look like you need this more than me."

"I'm fine," Ethan said, and picked up the cup, and his hand was steady, and the log was folded into his back pocket where he could feel the corner of it against the chair every time he shifted. He walked out with Mikaella as far as the stairwell, then stopped.

"I might skip the bus," he said.

"It's a twenty-minute walk."

"I know how long it is."

His father would be home by five. His grandfather took his reading at seven, in the chair by the window, in the same light every evening, and it occurred to Ethan that tonight he could be in the room when it happened, could watch the cuff inflate and deflate, could see the numbers arrive. He stood at the top of the stairs with the log's folded corner pressing into his pocket, and then he started down.

"Text me what he says," Mikaella called after him.

"Who?" Ethan said, already three steps below her, already moving.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and lilies, and Christian sat in the third row of folding chairs with his cap balanced on his knee. Mr. Holloway had lined them up alphabetically at the door, checking names off a clipboard, and when he reached DeMarcus and found an empty slot he had paused for a second, then moved on. Christian noticed. He kept noticing things like that today, the way you notice a draft only after someone points at the window.

Principal Something-or-Other gave a speech about doors opening. Christian's father had given a different speech that morning at the kitchen table, shorter: "You did what half the guys you started with couldn't." Christian hadn't argued, but the number sat wrong with him all through the processional, and when Keeley slid into the chair beside him, whispering that Adrien had saved them seats at the back of the party later, he leaned over and said, "It's not half."

"What?"

"Nothing. After."

The ceremony took ninety minutes. When his name was called, Christian crossed the stage, shook Mr. Holloway's hand, and felt the diploma's cardboard weight, lighter than a phone.

The party was in the same gymnasium, tables of sheet cake along the far wall, streamers sagging from the basketball hoops. Adrien had claimed a table near the water fountains and had already worked through two slices. "To the surviving polity," he said, raising a plastic cup of punch, because Adrien liked words he'd just learned. "The class of leaders, future captains of industry."

"Say that again but smaller," Keeley said.

"I'm being grandiose. It's graduation. You're allowed."

Christian pulled a folding chair around backward and sat with his arms across its back. "Keeley. You remember ninth grade. How many were in our homeroom?"

"Like thirty." She was peeling the paper off her cup. "Why."

"Count who's here."

She counted, lips moving, scanning the gym. Then she said, "Weller's not here. Barnes transferred junior year. The Reyes kid, the one with the skateboard, he stopped coming. Sato moved, I think, but Weller should be here." She set the cup down. "Devon Weller should be here."

Christian had looked it up in April, on a night when the college deposits were due and he couldn't sleep. He'd typed the phrase into his phone and found the number, and it had enervated him more than any rejection letter, drained something out of him that the acceptance emails didn't put back. "The national average," he said now. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. That's the real number. Not half. Thirteen out of a hundred gone, somewhere."

"That's us," Adrien said. "We're the eighty-seven."

"You make it sound like a scoreboard." Christian turned the chair a quarter turn so he was facing both of them. "My dad says the same thing. You finish, that's the whole game, the guys who didn't finish made their choice. But Weller's mom was sick. He was working at the tire place nights. What kind of choice is that?"

"A hard one," Keeley said.

"His dad would say the diploma's just a receipt," Adrien said. "Proof you paid. It doesn't mean the guys without receipts didn't pay."

They ate cake for a while after that. Christian watched Mr. Holloway near the stage, gathering the leftover programs, and thought about how his father's way of seeing and whatever this other way was didn't actually cancel each other out. He had earned the thing in his hand; he could be proud of that without pretending the empty chairs were empty because everyone in them deserved emptiness. Both of those could be true at once. What he couldn't figure out was what he was supposed to do about it, whether pride with an asterisk was still pride or just a smaller, more careful thing, and he didn't pretend to know.

He got up, crossed the gym, and took half the stack of programs from Mr. Holloway's arms.

"You don't have to do that, Christian."

"I know." He squared the programs against his chest. "Is there an address for the Weller family anywhere? In the office, I mean. In the files."

Mr. Holloway looked at him over the stack for a long moment. "There's a forwarding address," he said. "It's two years old."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: François Furet's 1978 book, translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, argued the French should stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history.
story:
Simon had the whole thing under control, which was why he was on his fourth game of solitaire at eleven in the morning. The essay was due Thursday. It was Tuesday. He had a thesis, more or less, in the sense that he had a document open with the word "Thesis" at the top of it, followed by nine minutes of blinking cursor. Ms. Saleh had assigned a historiographical essay, a word Simon had pretended to know for a full week before looking it up: not what happened in 1789, but what historians had been saying about it since. He'd underlined that distinction twice, which felt like work, and rewarded himself with solitaire.

His grandfather was at the kitchen table doing the crossword, retired and therefore free to be a permanent fixture of the house between six a.m. and whenever he felt like leaving. "What are you actually doing up there," he called, without looking up. "You've been sighing at that screen for an hour."

"Historiography," Simon said, because it sounded impressive and because it was technically true.

"Say it in French, then."

Simon came down and made toast he didn't want, mostly to be doing something with his hands. "It's about how people's views of the French Revolution changed. Like, since 1800."

"Robespierre," his grandfather said, with the satisfaction of a man retrieving a fact from deep storage. "A demagogue if there ever was one. They cut his head off too, in the end. Your grandmother loved that part."

"Nobody's arguing about whether it happened. They're arguing about what it meant." Simon tore his toast into smaller and smaller pieces. "For ages the French treated the Revolution as the thing that explains everything. Modern France, left and right, the whole works. Then this guy Furet wrote a book in 1978, it got translated as Interpreting the French Revolution, and he basically said, stop. Stop treating the Revolution as the key to all of modern French history."

"And instead?"

"Instead it's just one thing among others. It doesn't unlock everything." Simon heard how it sounded and shrugged. "I know it sounds small. It started a huge fight."

Nova arrived at noon, belligerent with sleep deprivation, carrying three energy drinks and a laptop with a cracked hinge. They had agreed to draft together, an arrangement that historically meant Nova worked and Simon narrated his intentions. She dropped onto the couch and opened Ms. Saleh's assignment sheet. "She wants competing schools," she said. "Marxist interpretation, revisionist, whatever came after. You've got Furet?"

"I've got Furet," Simon said, and he did, more or less, in the sense that he had a PDF and an opinion.

"Then you accede to the revisionists and we're done by four."

"That's the problem, though." He pulled the laptop toward himself and actually began typing, which surprised them both. "The Marxist historians thought the Revolution was the start of the modern class struggle, the bourgeoisie taking power. Furet's side said that's a story we told ourselves, that 1789 wasn't a train station all of history passes through. But then you read the after-Furet people and they can't agree either. Some of them basically put class back in through a side door."

"So pick a side."

"I'm saying maybe the honest thing is that nobody's won." He typed a sentence, deleted half of it, kept the rest. "Furet said stop looking for the key, and fifty years later everyone's still looking, just pretending they're not."

Nova drank half a can and looked at him with something between respect and suspicion, since Simon volunteering effort was roughly as common as snow in June. They worked through the afternoon in the way that actually works, arguing in fragments, Nova pushing him whenever his claims got more confident than his evidence. At one point she said, "You're sure the book's from 1978?" and Simon, who had been sure of many things that week without checking, actually checked. It was. He felt obscurely vindicated, as though the fact had held still for him out of courtesy.

By six he had eight hundred words and a conclusion he half believed: that the historiography wasn't a march toward truth so much as a series of disagreements that each revealed something the previous one had missed, and that a student essay could sit honestly inside that uncertainty without pretending to resolve it. He read it over twice. It was, he thought, probably the best thing he'd written, possibly the best thing anyone had written.

His grandfather appeared behind him with his coat on, ready to leave, and read the title over Simon's shoulder for a long moment. "So what's the key to the whole thing, then?" he asked.

"That's the point," Simon said. "There isn't one."

His grandfather nodded slowly, put on his hat, and paused at the door. "Your mother said the same thing at your age," he said. "Then she became a lawyer."

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Since 1975, ending most debate in the US Senate through cloture has required three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled.
story:
The bus smelled of orange peel and hairspray, and by the time they reached the legislature Sarah had heard the word "cloture" mispronounced four different ways. Their class had spent three weeks on how a bill became a law, which meant Ms. Katz had made them draft one. Sarah's group had proposed mandatory later start times for high schools, on the theory that teenagers were biologically nocturnal, a theory her father had denigrated over dinner as "an excuse invented by people who stay up texting." She had argued back with a printed study. He had not read it, which she suspected was the point.

Inside, the marble made everyone whisper. A guide walked them past the chamber doors while a page carried a folder of amendments down the corridor with the gravity of a courier bearing treaties. Bree leaned against a railing and said, "It's just paper going into rooms." Sarina, who wanted to be a lobbyist someday and said so the way other people said they were allergic to shellfish, said, "It's paper that decides when you have to get up."

They filed into a committee hearing on a school-lunch bill. A senator with a mannerism of clicking his pen before each sentence testified that the current nutrition standards were "adequate," a word Sarah had come to distrust, since it usually meant someone had stopped asking questions. A farmer in a brown corduroy jacket disagreed at length. The committee chair, impervious to both, called the vote, and the bill moved forward on a count of six to three, and Sarah felt something small and unexpected, a flutter of process working, of a thing being carried from hand to hand toward becoming real.

Then a student, not from her school, raised a hand during the question period and asked why a bill with fifty-five supporters in the Senate had failed last year. He said it like an accusation. The guide started to answer with something rehearsed about the flow of democracy, and Sarah, who had written a paper on this exact thing two months ago, felt the answer rise in her before she could decide whether to say it.

"Cloture," she said, too loud, and then at a normal volume, because everyone had turned. "Ending most debate in the Senate. Since 1975 it takes three-fifths of the senators. Sixty votes, if all hundred seats are filled." The guide blinked, recovered, and confirmed it with the mild deflation of a magician whose trick has been announced.

Afterward, in the rotunda, Bree said, "So fifty-five people wanting something isn't enough." She said it flatly, testing the weight of it. "That's either the smartest rule ever made or the worst one."

"Both," Sarina said. "It depends who's in the fifty-five."

Sarah had spent her whole paper arguing the second half of that, that the rule was a choke point dressed up as deliberation. She had written the phrase "minority tyranny" and underlined it. But standing under the dome, watching pages cross the marble with their folders, she kept thinking about the farmer in the corduroy jacket, who had talked for forty minutes and changed at least one vote she'd counted. Debate had done that. The same mechanism that killed bills she liked was the one that had kept that hearing from being a rubber stamp.

She tried to say this and it came out as, "I don't know anymore," which was not what she'd meant, or was exactly what she'd meant.

"That's very convincing," Bree said. "You should testify."

Later they were allowed to sit in the gallery while the full chamber took up the school-lunch bill, amended now in ways the farmer would not recognize. A senator rose to denigrate the amendments as "sausage," and another rose to defend sausage, and Sarah found herself tracking the votes as they were called, noting names, imagining each one traveling back to a district where someone had gotten up early to complain about tater tots. The bill passed on second reading. There would be a third reading, then the other chamber, then, if it survived all of that, something called assent, a final signing, a bill becoming a law, the whole apparatus of it visible at once like the inside of a clock.

On the bus home, Sarina drafted a letter to their state senator about school start times, using the word "circadian" twice. Bree slept against the window. Sarah wrote nothing. She kept thinking about the number sixty, how it was neither a majority nor a courtesy, how it sat there in the middle of everything, deciding, and how she had defended it and attacked it in the same day without resolving which she believed. The later-start-times bill, she decided, would need fifty-five friends and then five more, and she began, in the margin of Sarina's letter, to count.

"Circadian," Bree said suddenly, not opening her eyes. "Twice."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
The church hall smelled of wax and cut stems, and Noemie stood at the door holding a bundle of orange marigolds wrapped in newspaper, feeling like she had brought the wrong thing to the right place. Her grandmother had died in September, three weeks before Noemie left for college, and now it was the first of November and the parish was building an ofrenda at the front of the sanctuary, a long table draped in white where families could set photographs and bread and sugar skulls. Ms. Rowe, who organized everything at St. Augustine's, had told her to bring flowers. She had not said which kind.

She found Rafael at the table, arranging candles around a framed picture of his grandfather. He looked up at the bundle in her arms and frowned, not unkindly. "Where did you get those?"

"The bodega on Fifth. They had a bucket outside." She set them down and began to unwrap them, and only then did she notice that the heads were pale, more gold than orange, and that a few had gone brown at the edges, the way supermarket flowers do.

Rafael picked one up and turned it over. "These aren't cempasúchil," he said. "Not really. My mom would call these rejectas." He said it lightly, but she felt it land somewhere below her ribs.

"I didn't know there was a specific one." She was aware of how that sounded, an excuse, and she hated it. Her grandmother had been the Mexican half of her family, the half that lived eight hundred miles away in a house that smelled of cedar and burnt sugar, and Noemie had spent four summers there and learned to make tortillas by hand but never, apparently, learned this. Or maybe she had learned it once, at seven or eight, from a story at bedtime, and it had slid out of her the way childhood things do.

"There is," Rafael said. "The orange ones, the bright ones. On Day of the Dead the scent and the color are supposed to guide the souls home. My abuela used to make a path of petals from the front door to the altar so he wouldn't get lost." He set the flower down carefully, as if it were not quite a rejecta after all.

She looked at the table, at the photographs of strangers' dead, and tried not to dichotomize it into her side and his side, Mexican and not, grandchild who knew and grandchild who didn't. That was the lazy sorting her mind wanted to do, and it wasn't true. Her grandmother had loved orange; she had painted her kitchen orange one reckless summer and repainted it cream the following spring, and had laughed about it for years. If any color could find her, it should have been that one.

The bodega was six blocks away and the light was already going amber over the rooftops. "I'll go back," she said. "The flower district stalls stay open late this week." She was out the door before Rafael could answer, walking fast, and on the way she called her mother, who answered on the second ring with the sound of a kettle behind her.

"Do you remember if Abuela ever did the marigold thing? The path of petals?" Her mother was quiet for a moment, and Noemie braced for a story about cedar houses and old traditions, something that would make the whole afternoon tangential, a detour around the real thing, which was that her grandmother was gone and Noemie had left for school before anyone thought to say a proper goodbye.

"Once," her mother said. "The year after your grandfather died. But Noemie, she stopped after that. She said it was for people who believed their dead needed directions." A pause. "She believed he already knew the way."

At the flower stall on Sixth, under strings of white lights, she found them: crates of cempasúchil, so orange they seemed to hold their own light, the scent rising dense and dusty and sweet, nothing like the thin bodega bunches. She bought two armfuls and carried them back through the dark, petals shivering loose along the sidewalk behind her like a trail she was laying down without meaning to, and she thought about what her mother had said. Maybe the flowers were a map and maybe they were a decoration and maybe the difference didn't matter, maybe what mattered was that someone had wanted, badly, for the dead to find them. That was the part she could stand behind. Whether it worked was a question she could hold without answering, the way she was learning to hold most of the important ones.

In the sanctuary the candles had multiplied while she was gone. Rafael had cleared a space at the end of the table, next to his grandfather's photograph, and he raised his eyebrows at her two armfuls of orange. She set them down and pulled the framed picture of her grandmother from her bag, the one from the cedar house, the kitchen orange behind her and her hands floury, laughing at whoever held the camera. Then she snapped the stems short and began laying the flowers in a line across the cloth, from the edge of the table toward the photograph, a small path, a few feet of brightness.

"Your mom told you that thing about directions?" Rafael asked, watching her.

"She said Abuela didn't need them." Noemie set the last stem down and touched the frame, once, lightly. "These are for me, then. In case I'm the one who needs guiding home."

Behind them, a bell in the tower began to ring the hour, and the candle flames all leaned the same direction.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is 50,000 pounds or more.
story:
Lucas had commandeered the corner of Mr. Brown's garage where the workbench met the deep-freeze, spreading both leases across the plywood and weighting their corners with tins of half-used screws. The fluorescent tube overhead buzzed in a way he'd stopped hearing after the first hour, and the smell of machine oil and cold dust had settled into his jacket. Camryn sat on an upturned crate, holding the second lease open at the fees page while Anderson leaned against the freezer eating crisps he'd brought without offering around.

"Read me the rent again," Lucas said. "Both of them."

"The one on Albemarle Road is nine hundred a month. The one near the campus is eight hundred and twenty." Camryn turned the page against the draught from under the door. "But the campus one makes you pay water and internet on top, and the Albemarle one includes water but not leccy."

Anderson crumpled the packet one-handed. "So the cheap one isn't cheap. Story of my life."

Lucas drew a line down the back of an envelope. He had learned, over three evenings in this garage, that the whole exercise was a kind of translation: every flat spoke its own dialect of charges, and the only honest comparison was in totals. He wrote the rent, then the utilities the letting agents had quoted him by phone that afternoon, the water rates, the broadband, an estimate for electric he marked with a question mark because the agent had said "depends on your usage" in the tone of someone washing her hands of it.

"The deposit's where it gets weird," Camryn said. She read from the Albemarle lease, slowly. "A deposit of one thousand three hundred and eighty-seven pounds is payable on signing."

Lucas did the arithmetic on the envelope before he understood why he was doing it. Nine hundred a month, times twelve, was ten thousand eight hundred, well under fifty thousand. Five weeks of rent, at nine hundred a week over four and a third, came to about one thousand and thirty-five. He checked it twice, his pencil hovering over the figure like it might change under him.

"That's too much," he said. "By quite a lot."

"Too much how?" Anderson came off the freezer and looked over his shoulder, crisp dust still on his fingers.

"It's capped. In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds. Six weeks when it's fifty thousand or more." Lucas tapped the envelope. "Ours is under, so five weeks. Five weeks on nine hundred is a thousand and thirty-five, not one thousand three hundred and eighty-seven."

"Where'd you learn that?"

"Mr. Brown." Lucas nodded toward the door that joined the garage to the house, where the radio murmured through the wall with its diurnal rhythm of news and phone-ins. "I asked him about deposits on Tuesday and he printed something off. He wouldn't tell me what it meant, though. He said work it out yourself, you're the one moving out." The printout was folded in Lucas's back pocket, and he took it out now and smoothed it beside the leases, the paragraphs dense and official, the numbers exactly where he'd found them.

Camryn was already recalculating for the campus flat. "Eight hundred twenty a month. Five weeks on that is nine hundred and forty-five. Their deposit is nine hundred." She looked up. "That one's fine. Actually under."

"So the expensive flat is breaking the rule and the cheap one isn't," Anderson said, "which is the opposite of everything else about them."

Lucas sat back on the stool and looked at the two columns on the envelope. The campus flat came out cheaper in monthly totals once he'd added the utilities, though not by enough to settle it, and the electric estimate could still swing either way. The Albemarle flat was bigger, quieter, further from everything, and its landlord appeared to be asking for a deposit three hundred and fifty pounds over the legal cap. He didn't know yet whether that was an error or a habit, and he didn't know whether pointing it out would get it lowered or get the flat taken off the table entirely, because he had heard what happened sometimes when you told a landlord the law.

He pulled his phone out and found the agent's number, the one who had said depends on your usage in that rinsed-out voice.

"You're going to ring them now?" Camryn said. "It's half eight."

"I'm going to email them the numbers," Lucas said, "and ask which the deposit is supposed to be." He began typing, his thumb slow and deliberate on each word, while the fluorescent tube buzzed on above the envelope and its two uneven columns.

"Send it to me after," Camryn said. "I want to see what they say."

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together.
story:
The car smelled like cardboard and his mother's coffee, and Austin had his knees against the seatback because the boxes left him no room. They had been on the interstate for an hour when his phone buzzed and he saw it was Deacon, calling for the third time since the parking lot.

"You're going to have to answer him eventually," his mother said, eyes on the road.

"I know." He let it ring out. At the going-away thing last night, in Kyana's backyard, Deacon had made a joke about Austin's new town, something about corn and nothing else, and Austin had laughed along, and then Deacon had kept going, listing everything Austin was abandoning, and nobody laughed at the last one. Austin had said something sharp back. He couldn't remember the exact words, which was the worst part, because now he couldn't take back a specific thing. He only knew the shape of what he'd said, which was: fine, go ahead, replace me.

Kyana had texted at midnight: just call him tomorrow. He had not called him tomorrow. Now tomorrow was a highway.

He watched the guardrails flick past and thought about a fact he'd read in Mr. Haddad's classroom, on one of the posters Mr. Haddad never talked about but never took down. Jeffrey Hall's 2018 study had estimated that becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. Austin had done the arithmetic once, bored in the back row: he and Deacon had known each other since seventh grade. Practices, bus rides, basements, the summer of the broken AC when they'd sequestered themselves in the library with the good air conditioning for whole afternoons. Two hundred hours was nothing. They had banked thousands. And Kyana too, Kyana who had sat with him through his grandfather's funeral even though she hadn't known his grandfather, Kyana who was already claiming she'd visit in October.

His phone buzzed again. Deacon.

"Take it," his mother said. "I'll be quiet."

He answered. There was a silence long enough that he heard the turn signal, his mother drifting one lane over.

"I was kidding," Deacon said finally. "About the corn."

"I know you were kidding."

"You didn't act like it."

Austin looked out at a water tower with a faded team name on it, some town he would never live in, and understood that the fight wasn't really about corn, and that both of them knew that, and that saying so out loud would cost something. He tried anyway. "It felt like you were already letting go of me. Like you wanted to be the one who ended it first."

Deacon was quiet again. Then: "Mr. Haddad's poster. The one about 200 hours. I keep thinking about that."

"The 2018 study."

"Yeah. Jeffrey Hall. Becoming close friends takes more than 200 hours spent together. I did the math on us. It's so much more than that. So I figured it doesn't just, like, evaporate." Deacon's voice did something at the end, a small crack he tried to cover with a cough. "But then I thought, I don't actually know how it works. Nobody does. That's kind of what freaks me out. You could have all the hours in the world and still drift."

Austin felt the truth of that land somewhere under his ribs. He had been treating the move like a cliff, a clean fall, when it was probably more like weather, gradual and evanescent and impossible to watch happening. He hated that answer. He wanted either the cliff or a guarantee, and neither was on offer.

"So I was thinking," Deacon said, "we schedule it. Not wait and see. Like, Tuesdays, you call me, and Sundays I call you, and if one of us misses it, no drama, we just do the next one. Build the hours on purpose. It's not the same as the basement. I know that."

"It's a plan," Austin said. "It's a bad plan that's better than no plan." His mother was pretending not to listen, and pretending badly, smiling at the windshield.

"It's the plan I have," Deacon said.

"Then it's the plan." Austin read the mile marker out loud to him, for no reason except that Deacon would want to know where he was, and Deacon said to read the next one too, and the next, until Kyana beeped in on the other line, and Austin said hold on, I'm putting us both together, hang on.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: The development typically breaks the exposition's themes into short fragments and moves them quickly through several keys, which gives the section its restless sound.
story:
The assignment sheet said the quiz would ask them to mark, on a blank listening sheet, where the exposition ended and the recapitulation began, and Matthew had been putting it off for four days. Now it was Sunday night, the kitchen table cleared of dinner, his headphones plugged into his mother's laptop, and Mozart's Sonata in A major, K. 331, first movement, sitting in the file like something waiting to betray him. He pressed play.

The opening tune arrived all sweetness, a lilting phrase that repeated and varied itself, and he wrote "A" for theme one in his notebook and underlined it twice. For a while he felt competent, even smug. Then the music turned. The left hand dropped into something rolling and low, the right hand hurried, and the tune he had loved was simply gone, replaced by arpeggios that seemed to be searching for a room they had already left. He paused the recording, wrote "development???", and stared at the three question marks until they stopped meaning anything.

He texted Willyam, who had taken the same quiz section last year. Willyam replied with a shrug emoji and the message, "honestly i just guessed. ismail actually studied tho." Ismail answered on the second try: "skipping? i can call after eight. family thing now." Matthew sat with the silence of the kitchen, the dishwasher humming its own bass line, and did what he always did when he could not solve something, which was to introspect until the problem either opened or shut. It shut. The middle section was a storm, and he could not find a single landmark in it.

His mother came down in her painting clothes, the ones that smelled faintly of turpentine, and set a mug of tea beside his elbow without asking. "Is that your Mozart thing," she said. It wasn't a question. She stood behind him for a moment, looking over his shoulder at the notebook, at the three question marks, and he felt the old childish urge to cover the page. "When I was little," she said, "we had a house on the coast, and the tide would take the whole beach away and bring it back twice a day. Same beach." She tapped the top of his page, above the storm. "Maybe stop trying to hear the beach and listen for what the water's carrying." Then she went back upstairs, which was her way of not being a teacher about it.

At eight-fifteen his phone buzzed and Ismail's voice filled his other ear, slightly echoey, calling from his father's shop. "Okay, so Ms. Jean-Louis played it three times for us," Ismail said, "and the trick is you don't listen for the whole tune. The development takes the exposition's themes and smashes them into these little pieces, right, and it moves them through a bunch of different keys really fast. That's why it sounds so restless. You're not supposed to feel at home there." Matthew wrote down what Ismail had said, word for word almost, and then sat without moving. It was like being told that the shore he was standing on was littoral by nature, always the edge of something else, never a place itself.

He played the storm again from the beginning, slower this time in his attention if not in fact. Six bars in, the left hand growled out a figure in F sharp minor, four notes, quick, and something in the back of his mind lifted its head. He rewound. Four notes: the last four notes of the opening tune, the ones that had ended each sweet phrase like a signature, except now they were hurled into a minor key and passed immediately to another key, then another, as if someone were carrying a photograph through a series of unfamiliar houses. He heard it again two bars later, upside down, in the right hand. The tune had not been destroyed. It had been broken on purpose and scattered.

"Do you hear this," he said to Ismail, who was still on the line. He held the phone up to the headphone cup, which he knew was ridiculous, and Ismail laughed. "You found it, didn't you." "It's everywhere," Matthew said. "She hid it in the storm." He marked the spot in his notebook, drew a small box around the four notes, and wrote "opening tune!" beside it, and then, because the section kept modulating, kept refusing to settle, he found three more fragments and boxed those too, the page beginning to look like evidence at a trial. He still didn't know exactly where the development began or where the recapitulation would return; that was the thing he could not yet answer, and he was honest enough with himself to write that in the margin. Returning, maybe. He would have to listen for the beach coming back.

When the opening tune finally did return, whole and unharmed, in the original key, he felt something loosen in his chest that he had not known was tight. He did not write a lesson in his notebook. He underlined "recapitulation," checked the clock, saw it was past ten, and played the whole movement once more from the top, pencil hovering over the blank sheet, waiting for the water to change.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A LEFT JOIN in SQL returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists.
story:
The library closed at six, and Jeremy had until then to make the query work. Mr. Lau, the reference librarian who let students use the back computers after school, had already warned him twice that the lab competition entries were due by email at eight that night, and the clock on the wall above the printers showed 4:37. Jeremy spread his notes across the desk: a printed table of customers, a printed table of orders, and a practice problem from the county's data skills contest that read, in flat black type, "Write a query that lists every customer along with their orders. Then identify which customers ordered nothing."

Annabelle dropped into the chair beside him with two granola bars and read the problem upside down. "That's a trick, right? There's nothing to find. If they ordered nothing, they're not in the orders table at all."

"That's what I thought." Jeremy pulled the keyboard closer. "So then the answer is just, take the customers who aren't in orders. Except I don't know how to ask for a thing that isn't there." He typed his first attempt anyway, a plain join, and ran it. The screen filled with rows: every customer who had ever bought something, matched to what they bought. He counted them. Eleven. The customers table held fourteen.

Maxim arrived with his backpack still on one shoulder, chewing the cap of a pen. "You're missing three," he said, leaning over Jeremy's shoulder. The heater under the window ticked, and somewhere behind the stacks a cart of returned books squeaked along the carpet.

"Look at this one." Jeremy opened the tutorial Mr. Lau had printed for him from the library database, and there it was, a line of example syntax with a phrase he'd skimmed past twice. He read it slowly, then typed it out, hands a little unsteady. The result appeared in the lower pane: fourteen rows. Three of them had a customer name, and then, in the order columns, the word NULL, printed small and gray in each empty cell.

"NULL," Annabelle said. "What does that even mean, nothing?"

Jeremy traced the row with his finger. "It means no matching row exists. Those three customers have no orders, so their order columns are empty." He scrolled down, then up, checking the count again. "The join puts every single customer in, even the ones with nothing, and fills in the blank with NULL." The exhilaration hit him all at once, and he sat back, grinning at the little gray word like it was a door someone had left unlocked.

"So those three are your answer," Maxim said, tapping the screen. "Customers who ordered nothing. You just look for the NULLs."

"But which way did it go?" Jeremy asked. He was thinking of his older sister, who worked at a pharmacy and had once spent a whole evening explaining that direction mattered, that you had to know which shelf you were counting from. He moved the table names, swapped their positions in the query, and ran it again. This time the rows changed: he got only the customers who had orders, and the customers with nothing dropped out entirely. He swapped them back, and the NULLs returned. "It depends on the order," he said slowly. "One table is on the left of the join. Every row from that left table shows up, and the NULLs appear wherever the right table has no match." He wrote it down in his notebook under the heading the tutorial used: LEFT JOIN. He underlined left twice.

Annabelle cracked open a granola bar and offered him half. "So is that your answer, or are you still not sure?"

"I'm sure about the three customers," Jeremy said. "I'm not sure I could explain why the left table gets to keep everything and the right one doesn't. Not past what I just saw." He looked at the clock: 5:12. He had the answer, and something close to a reason, and he could feel the difference between them. He began typing the final version, checking each column name against the printout, while Maxim read the syntax over his shoulder and Annabelle folded the empty granola wrapper into a tight little square.

At 5:40 he hit run one last time, copied the output into the entry form, and clicked send. The confirmation banner appeared in green. Mr. Lau came by on his rounds, saw the screen, and said, "Closing in twenty minutes, gentlemen." Jeremy saved his file to the cloud, then sat for a moment with his hands still on the keyboard, looking at the three gray NULLs.

"I'm going to reread that whole chapter tonight," he said. "Just to see if it says anything else true that I've been skipping."

Annabelle zipped her jacket. "Then you can teach it to me in study hall."

"I can try," Jeremy said, and logged off.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The Maillard reaction, between amino acids and sugars, browns food and creates much of its flavor; it proceeds rapidly at about 140 to 165 degrees Celsius.
story:
Violet had promised her grandmother a proper dinner by the time the family arrived at six, and by five the chicken was already a problem. She had followed the recipe taped inside the cupboard, the one in her grandmother's small, sloping hand, and the pieces had come out of the steaming pan pale as parchment, releasing water instead of sizzling, their surfaces slack and grey. Her grandmother stood at the doorway with her walker and said nothing, which was worse than criticism. Violet poked one thigh with a fork and watched liquid pool in the dent.

"Grandma," she said, "it's cooked through. It's just nothing."

Her grandmother came closer, leaning on the counter, and looked at the pan the way she looked at a misprint in the crossword. "It's called the Maillard reaction," she said. "Amino acids and sugars. That's what browns it. That's where the flavor comes from." She tapped the edge of the pan with one knuckle, once. "You kept the heat too low."

Violet turned the dial off and stood in the sudden quiet of the fan winding down. She had steamed the chicken politely, the way she did most things lately, at a temperature that couldn't hurt anyone. Somewhere between 140 and 165 degrees Celsius, she remembered from chemistry, that browning ran fast; below it, nothing. She had been miles below it.

"I can fix it," she said. "There's another pack in the fridge."

"There's another pack in the fridge," her grandmother agreed, and lowered herself into the chair by the window to supervise, which meant to doze with one eye open.

Violet texted Imane a photo of the pale chicken, then, when the family was forty minutes out and the second batch was drying on towels, a photo of the new pieces hitting a pan hot enough that the oil shivered and slid. Imane replied first with a vomiting emoji and then: "morphology of that first one is a crime. pale chicken is a malevolent force. use butter." Violet laughed, typed back a rude reply, and copied the advice, adding a knob of it to the pan.

The smell changed before the color did. It went from damp nothing to something toasted and sweet at the edges, and the thighs darkened in rings where they touched the iron. Her grandmother opened both eyes.

"There it is," she said.

While the chicken rested, Violet found the note. It had been waiting under the fruit bowl all afternoon, she realized later; her grandmother must have written it before Violet even arrived. It was addressed to her in pencil, on the back of a grocery receipt.

Violet,

If you are reading this the chicken came out pale again, or you are snooping while it rests, which is more like you. When your grandfather was alive he boiled everything. Forty years of grey pork. I never told him what I am telling you, because he liked his way and I liked him. But you, I think, would rather know. Hotter pan. Dry the pieces. Let it brown. Do not put it in the oven and abscond to your phone. People want dinner but what they want more is to be waited on a little. You are good at that part already.

Love, Grandma.

P.S. There are peas in the freezer.

The letter was a small strange thing to Violet, her grandmother having anticipated a failure and forgiven it in advance, and she read it twice, and then, because the peas needed starting, she put it in her apron pocket. She thought of her mother arriving, of her uncle who always hovered near the stove, of the first chicken sitting in the trash like a verdict. She thought too of Imane's message, butter and honesty, and of Ms. Silva, who had told them in the spring that a good experiment was one where you learned something even when it went wrong. She wasn't sure that was entirely true yet. She had learned something; she had also made everyone wait. Both of those would be true at six o'clock, and she would have to hold them at the same time.

From the chair by the window, her grandmother watched Violet move around the kitchen without hurrying, draining the peas, carving the browned chicken with the electric knife, putting the carved pieces back in the warm pan so they wouldn't cool on the platter. The girl had her father's way of going quiet when she was concentrating, jaw set, and her grandmother found she was not thinking about the chicken at all. She was thinking about the note and whether she had said too much in it, whether waiting on people was a lesson or just an inheritance, whether you could teach a girl to run a kitchen without teaching her that the kitchen was where she belonged. She did not know the answer. She put her hand flat on the table to steady herself for standing.

When the family came through the door, cold air and noise and the dog first, the table was already set, and Violet carried the platter out with both hands, steam rising off the browned skin, the letter still folded in her apron pocket, and her grandmother called from her chair, "Tell them about the Maillard reaction, Violet. Tell them why it tastes like that."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
The cones in the driving school lot were spaced to codify the exact dimensions of a parked car, and Mackenzie had clipped three of them in a row. "You're not steering," said Ms. Cardinal from the passenger seat, her clipboard balanced on one knee. "You're apologizing with the wheel." Mackenzie pulled forward again, checked her mirrors, and tried to let the steering wheel turn under her palms instead of wrestling it toward the curb like it owed her something. The fourth attempt brought the rear tyre within a hand's width of the kerb, close enough that she held her breath, waiting to be told whether touching it would have ruined everything.

That was the question she could not stop carrying around. On Tuesday, in the school library, she had overheard Sara and Freya arguing about the practical test. Sara was adamant that one small mistake, one kiss of the kerb, meant automatic failure. Freya laughed at her, in that way Freya had of being facetious precisely when someone was frightened, and said that if that were true nobody in the country would have a licence. Neither of them actually knew. They had traded confidence back and forth like it was the same thing as information, and Mackenzie, who had her test booked for the following month, had gone home and looked it up herself.

What she found surprised her. A candidate could pass with up to fifteen driving faults. It was only serious or dangerous faults that ended things immediately. She read it twice, because it did not match her instincts at all. She had been thinking of the test as a kind of syntax, a rigid grammar where a single wrong symbol broke the whole sentence. Apparently the examiners had built in room for the ordinary human texture of error, fifteen whole imperfections allowed, and the line was drawn somewhere else entirely, at faults that actually put people in danger. She sat with that for a while, wondering which of her own mistakes were merely wrong and which were wrong in a way that mattered.

On Thursday she found out the difference in her hands. Ms. Cardinal took her out on the ring road for merging practice, and the first on-ramp went badly. Mackenzie accelerated too late, arrived at the end of the slip road doing forty with a lorry filling her mirror, and had to slow almost to a stop with her indicator blinking at an empty lane. "That," said Ms. Cardinal quietly, "is the kind of thing they call dangerous." Mackenzie's face went hot. She understood instantly. Clipping a cone in a car park was a driving fault, a tolerated flaw. Arriving at highway speed with nowhere to go was a different species of mistake, and no amount of permitted faults could absorb it.

The second on-ramp she got right, and the feeling of it stayed with her all week. She had looked down the slip road, matched her speed to the flow, and slid into a gap the way you slot a last piece into a puzzle, and for three seconds the whole system had made sense to her, the give and take of it, the way strangers made room for each other at speed because everyone understood the same unspoken rules. She had even mentioned it to Sara, who was still insisting that the test was designed to fail people. "You're allowed fifteen faults," Mackenzie told her. "Just not serious or dangerous ones." Sara had blinked, reassessed, and grudgingly said that maybe she would book her test after all, since apparently it wasn't the trap she'd imagined.

By the following lesson, Mackenzie had developed a small private theory, which was that everyone she knew divided the world the way Sara and Freya had divided the test. Some people thought any flaw was fatal; some thought nothing was fatal. Both of them were guessing. What she liked about the actual rule was its honesty, the way it admitted that competence and perfection were different things, that a good driver was not a flawless one. She didn't say any of this aloud, because saying it would have sounded like a poster, but it changed how she practised. She stopped trying to be perfect on the cones and started trying to be smooth, and strangely, the cones stopped falling.

Ms. Cardinal noticed. "Something's different," she said on Friday, watching Mackenzie reverse into the space between two cones with a slow, unhurried patience that would have been unthinkable two weeks earlier. "You've stopped punishing yourself." Mackenzie let the car settle, applied the handbrake, and looked at the gap she'd left between her rear wheel and the kerb. It was maybe four inches. On her very first lesson she had clipped that kerb and spent the whole drive home convinced she'd already failed some invisible test that hadn't even happened yet.

Her rear tyre was touching it. Not crushing, not riding up, just resting against the kerb like a hand on a shoulder, so lightly that she hadn't felt it through the wheel at all. Mackenzie stared at the mirror for a long moment, calculating. Fifteen faults allowed. She had used exactly one. "Well," she said to Ms. Cardinal, and found she was grinning instead of grimacing, "at least now I know what that costs." Ms. Cardinal leaned over, looked at the tyre, and made a small mark on her clipboard. "Thirteen more where that came from," she said. "Save them for the ones you can't predict."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Psychologist George Bonanno's research on bereaved people found that resilience is common, and that there are no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss.
story:
Levi stood in his grandfather's kitchen with a roll of packing tape and no idea where to start. The house smelled like coffee grounds and pencil shavings, the way it always had, and that seemed wrong, because his grandfather had been dead for six days and the smell had no right to persist. His mother was upstairs sorting sweaters into boxes marked KEEP and DONATE, and she had given Levi the kitchen and the study, the rooms with the most clutter, presumably to keep his hands busy. He opened a drawer and found a bread knife, three rubber bands, and a pad of graph paper covered in his grandfather's handwriting, which was small and fierce, like the man himself.

He had not cried yet. That was the problem, if it was a problem. At the funeral he had held his mother's elbow and looked suitably grave, and then on Tuesday he had gone to school, and on Wednesday Erik had told a story about the vending machine in the science wing that only accepted nickels, and Levi had laughed so hard he had to leave the room. He kept waiting for the other thing, the heavy thing, the thing people in movies had. His aunt had already asked him twice how he was really doing, with a tone that suggested there was a correct answer, and he had lied both times and said fine.

He lifted a box of books off the study shelf and something slid out from between them, a softback textbook with a cracked spine: Introduction to Psychology, third edition. The provenance was obvious once he checked the inside cover, because his grandfather had written his own name there in blue ballpoint, dated the year after Levi's grandmother died. Levi sat down in the desk chair, which spun a little, and opened the book to a flagged page, because his grandfather flagged everything with torn strips of index card.

There was a chapter on bereavement, and in the margin, next to a passage about the psychologist George Bonanno, his grandfather had written a single word: wrong? Levi read the page twice. Bonanno had studied bereaved people and found that resilience was common, and that there were no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. The margin note did not say what was wrong, the idea or the man's own life, and Levi turned the book over as if the back cover might tell him.

He was still holding it when Mackenna knocked, two short raps, and let herself in the way she always had since they were nine. She had driven over after her afternoon class with a bag of Thai food and no expectation of being useful, which was exactly why she was useful. "Your mom said you were entombed in the study," she said. She looked at the open book in his lap. "Psych? I'm in psych. That's my class, actually."

"Grandpa's," Levi said. "From after Grandma died. He underlined this guy Bonanno, wrote wrong? next to it."

Mackenna leaned over his shoulder, chewing. "We just covered that. Bonanno followed people after losses and found resilience is common. And that there are no mandatory stages everyone has to pass through." She tapped the page. "Like, the famous stages. Half my class refused to believe it."

So there it was. And here was the part Levi could not stop turning over: he had spent a week believing he was grieving incorrectly, compartmentalizing school and jokes into one drawer and his grandfather into another, waiting for a curriculum of sorrow that everyone was supposedly issued. And his grandfather, a man who had been raised in a narrow sectarian church that graded grief like homework, had apparently read the same finding and written wrong? in the margin. Levi looked at the word again and understood, suddenly and without proof, that the question mark was not skepticism. It was his grandfather asking it about himself.

I turned to the last flagged page in the book, and there, on the inside back cover, was a note in the same blue ballpoint, undated: Bowling Thursday with R. First time since. Felt disloyal. Felt good. Levi read it four times. R was Ruben, his grandfather's friend from the machine shop, the one who had come to the funeral in a suit that clearly hurt him. His grandfather had gone bowling eleven days after his wife died, had laughed at something on the lane, and had needed to write down that the laughing and the missing could sit in the same man without canceling out.

I took out my phone and texted Erik: you free tomorrow, need to return your nickels joke with interest. Then I put the book in the KEEP box, and carried the box out to the car before my mother could weigh in on its provenance or anything else, and Mackenna stood in the doorway holding the Thai food like an offering.

"Yo, Sokolov's car is in your driveway," she said, squinting past me. Mr. Sokolov from down the lane, the neighbor my grandfather had feuded with for thirty years over a property line, was standing at the end of the walk with a casserole dish and the expression of a man who had practiced this in the mirror.

"You go ahead," I told Mackenna. "Save me the spring rolls." And I walked down the drive and took the dish out of his hands.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Under the two-second rule, a driver watches the car ahead pass a fixed point, such as a sign, and checks that at least two seconds pass before reaching that same point.
story:
Gabrielle had the wheel in a white-knuckled grip before the car even moved, and Ms. Gallagher, sliding into the passenger seat with her clipboard, said only, "Relax your thumbs, dear. The car can feel you." In the back seat, Felicia was already filming, which was either moral support or evidence for a later indictment, depending on how the next hour went. They had signed up together, the way you do things at seventeen, so that failure would at least have a witness.

The parking lot of the driving school was empty except for a row of orange cones that transfixed Gabrielle the moment she pulled out. She steered toward them as if they were the only fixed things in the world, and when Ms. Gallagher told her to turn left onto the road, the sudden openness of it made her hands go light on the wheel. A car ahead of them, a grey hatchback, sat at the light. Gabrielle crept forward until she could read the dealership sticker on its bumper.

"You're a bit close," Ms. Gallagher said, in the tone of someone noting the weather.

Gabrielle eased off, then drifted forward again at the next light without meaning to. Her foot had its own opinion. It happened a third time, and she saw Ms. Gallagher's hand settle quietly near the brake, and that small gesture stung more than a lecture would have. From the back seat, Felicia leaned forward. "Oskar failed his first test for that," she offered. "He calls it the two-second rule. He wouldn't shut up about it."

Ms. Gallagher said nothing, which Gabrielle was beginning to understand was the whole method. The instructor gave her the road and let her find the ditch. So Gabrielle thought about the phrase and looked out at the storefronts sliding past, and she tried an experiment. There was a lamppost coming up on the right. The grey hatchback passed it. She counted, one, and her own hood was already passing the same lamppost. One second. Maybe less.

"Again," she said to herself, and waited for the next fixed point, a stop sign half a block down. The hatchback passed the sign; she counted one, two, and only then did her car reach it, because she had let her foot off the gas a little, not braking, just releasing. It felt strange, deliberately falling behind, as if she were conceding something. She did it again with a fire hydrant, and again with the shadow line of an awning, and each time the gap stayed there, patient, the same size, no matter how fast they went. She began to see the street differently, as a series of points she could use, the way Felicia saw everything as content.

Then came the twist, and it arrived gently. They were stopped at a red light and Gabrielle glanced over at Ms. Gallagher, and the woman's lips were moving. Counting. Gabrielle watched for three full points, a mailbox, a painted crosswalk, a bus bench, and every time the car ahead passed one, Ms. Gallagher's mouth shaped one, two, right along with her. She had been counting the whole lesson, every road, probably every lesson, for years. The calm in the passenger seat was not the absence of fear. It was fear with a system on it.

The light turned green. Ahead, the hatchback's brake lights flared without warning, some driver late for a turn, and Gabrielle, three seconds back instead of one, had the time to lift her foot and drift to a smooth stop with room to spare. Nobody said anything for a moment. The space in front of her hood, ordinary and evanescent as any gap in traffic, held still.

"Did you see that?" Felicia said from the back, phone lowered at last. "Texted Oskar. He says you have to tell him exactly what you did."

Gabrielle checked the mirror, signalled, and pulled out around the turning car. "Tell him I counted a lamppost," she said. "Tell him I'm keeping the lamppost."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: 'Ibid.' abbreviates the Latin 'ibidem', meaning 'in the same place', and is used in a note citing the same source as the note just before it.
story:
Mr. Luo had booked the library's back room for the writing club every Thursday until five, and today he arrived carrying a photocopy so old it had gone the color of weak tea. "Footnotes," he announced, as though unveiling a criminal. "Also, your research papers are due Monday, which some of you appear to have forgotten."

Logan had not forgotten, exactly. He had been ruminating on his thesis about city bike-share programs for four days, which is different from writing, the way staring at a kettle is different from making tea. He had eleven sources, a half-formed argument, and zero footnotes. Beside him, Gracelyn slid a completed draft across the table like a card sharp, and Coen was on his fourth revision of his title page alone.

Mr. Luo passed around the photocopy, a page torn from some dissertation, dense text on top and a column of small print below. "Notice the apparatus at the bottom. Monday. Chicago style. Bibliography, properly formatted." He said this with the grim satisfaction of a man collecting a debt.

The page reached Logan last. He read the footnotes down the column and stopped. Note fourteen cited a book by a woman named Halloran. Note fifteen said, in its entirety, "Ibid., 47." Note sixteen: "Ibid., 52." Note seventeen: "Ibid." He turned the page over as if the rest of the sentence might be hiding there.

"What is this," he said. "Is it a typo? Did the printer run out of letters?"

"It's Latin," Gracelyn said, without looking up from her draft.

"So is my grandmother's tattoo and nobody explains that either."

Coen leaned over. "No, look. Where the Ibid. shows up, it means the same source as the note right before it. Ibidem. 'In the same place.'"

"That's allowed?" Logan said. "You can just write that?"

"That's the whole point of it," Gracelyn said. "Otherwise every note would be the same book over and over and your page would look like a phone book."
