Logan looked at the column again and felt the small, unreasonable joy of a person who has been handed a shortcut that is also legitimate. He had three quotes from the same city planning report. He had been dreading typing that report out four separate times, publisher and all, like a monk copying scripture.

The problem was time. Thursday, five o'clock, eleven sources, a thesis that currently read, in his notebook, "bikes: good? complicated." He stayed after the others left, spreading his notes across two tables, and Mr. Luo let him, grading essays at the end of the room with a red pen and an expression of professional melancholy.

By seven Logan had an argument, footnoted, that bike-share programs justified their public disbursement of funds only when stations crossed into lower-income neighborhoods, and he was proud of it in the way you are proud of a sandcastle before the tide. He typed his notes, and he used Ibid., and he used it again, and once he used it twice in a row because the same report kept giving him exactly the number he needed, like a friend who always has bus fare.

At home Friday he kept working, and somewhere past eleven at night, tired, he cut a paragraph about Copenhagen and pasted it into a different section, and did not check the notes that traveled with it.

Monday, Mr. Luo returned the papers. Logan's came back with a grade that made him wince and one comment circled twice in red: "Note 9: Ibid. referring to what? Note 8 is the wrong source. Check your sequence."

Logan sat down at lunch with the paper and a feeling like finding a sock in the wrong drawer. The paragraph had moved; the notes had not. His note eight now cited a magazine article, and his note nine, loyal to the end, said Ibid., pointing at the wrong thing entirely, confidently directing readers to a source that had never contained the sentence above it. His shortcut had betrayed him with total sincerity.

Gracelyn slid into the seat across from him with her tray. "Fixable?"

"One note," Logan said. "One lazy word that didn't know the paragraph had moved."

"Tragic," she said, and stole one of his fries. "Your bibliography's nice, though."

"You haven't read my bibliography."

"I skimmed it while Mr. Luo was talking about pagination." She shrugged. "It was either that or learn what a hanging indent is."

Logan pulled out his pen and fixed the note right there, crossing out the small word and writing the full citation in longhand, every letter of it, like a monk after all. Then he looked at the corrected page, at his terrible grade sitting next to his decent argument, and made a deal with himself out loud.

"Next paper, I check every note twice."

"Mm," said Gracelyn, through the fry.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The force on a charge in an electric field equals the charge times the field strength, F = qE, so doubling the charge doubles the force.
story:
Isla had promised Mr. Whitehead she would finish the physics worksheet before the field trip ended, and now there were only forty minutes left and one exhibit left unvisited. The electrostatics room occupied the museum's east wing, dim except for the amber glow of a demonstration case where two parallel metal plates sat facing each other like the covers of a closed book. Abigayle stood beside her with the worksheet folded into a paper crane, which was Abigayle's way of saying she had already given up.

"Read it to me again," Abigayle said, unfolding the crane with theatrical regret.

Isla read. Between two charged plates, the worksheet said, the electric field is uniform. Compute the field strength at a point between the plates, then use it. The numbers were on the placard beside the case: the plates were connected to a source that produced a potential difference of three hundred volts, and the plates were separated by two centimetres. Isla copied both numbers onto her palm in ballpoint ink.

"Divide," she said quietly. "Three hundred volts over two hundredths of a metre. That's fifteen thousand volts per metre." She said it again, testing the shape of it in her mouth, because it seemed strange that something so large could be hiding inside a case the size of a toaster oven.

Elliott had drifted over from the plasma ball with his hands still smelling faintly of the hand sanitizer by the elevators. He leaned over the case, not blase about it exactly, but performing indifference the way he did at parties, and asked why any of it mattered if the plates were just sitting there doing nothing. Abigayle pointed to the fine dust drifting inside the case, motes turning slowly above the lower plate, and said it wasn't doing nothing, look.

Isla looked. The dust was charged, the placard said; grains had picked up charge from touching the plate. She still needed a force, though, a push, something the worksheet would accept as an answer. She wrote F equals qE on her palm and stared at it. The field she had computed, fifteen thousand volts per metre, times the charge on a grain, would give the force on that grain. She tried it with the number the placard offered for a typical grain, and then, because she was curious rather than careful, she doubled the charge to see what would happen. The force doubled. Exactly, cleanly doubled, the way doubling ingredients doubles a recipe.

"So if I picked up twice as much charge," she said to no one in particular, "the push on me would be twice as strong. Force equals charge times field strength."

Elliott shrugged and said that sounded obvious, and Isla conceded it might be, but obvious things had never felt obvious to her until she had turned them over once. There was a version of herself, she thought, standing exactly here, that wanted to equivocate, to say well, it depends, maybe, in some cases. But it didn't depend. The force on a charge in this field was just the charge times the field, and a bigger charge got a proportionally bigger shove, and the direction of the shove followed the sign, one way for positive, the opposite for negative. She watched a grain near the upper plate drift down while a grain near the lower plate rose, and she wondered whether they carried opposite charges, and whether the field between the plates was truly uniform or whether the placard was simplifying for visitors like her.

"Do you think it's really the same everywhere in there?" she asked Abigayle. "Fifteen thousand volts per metre at every point?"

Abigayle said she thought museums lied a little to everyone, but kindly, the way a good tour guide does. Isla laughed and wrote her answer in the last blank on the worksheet, in careful print so Mr. Whitehead could read it: field strength fifteen thousand volts per metre; force on a grain of charge q equal to q times that; double the charge, double the force. She had drawn a small arrow beside each plate and labeled it with a question mark, because she was not certain which direction the field pointed, and she did not want to pretend she was. Honesty about the uncertainty felt like part of the answer rather than a failure of it.

Mr. Whitehead collected the worksheets near the bus, glancing at hers longer than at the others. "You doubled the charge," he said. "Why?"

"Because I wanted to see what the force would do," Isla said.

He looked at her for a moment, then at the small arrow with its question mark, and did not mark anything wrong. Behind him, through the glass doors, the museum's lights were going off wing by wing, and in her mind Isla could still see the dust turning in the amber glow, each grain being pushed in proportion to what it carried, and she wondered what it would feel like to be small enough to stand between those plates herself, and whether she would rise or fall.

Abigayle tugged her sleeve toward the bus. "Coming?"

"Coming," Isla said, and pocketed the pen.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: At the top of its path a projectile's vertical velocity is zero, but its horizontal velocity is not, so it is still moving.
story:
The playground at dusk had become their unofficial study hall, three textbooks balanced on a picnic table while the swings creaked in the wind behind them. Jordyn turned her physics worksheet face up and read the problem again: a ball launched at an angle, find its velocity at the highest point of its path. Beside her, Sloane tapped her pen against the table in an agitated rhythm.

"That one's a trick," Sloane said. "At the top, the ball stops. That's the whole point of the top. It goes up, it pauses, it comes down. So the velocity is zero. Done." She wrote a large zero on her paper and circled it, as if the circle could defend the answer from Ms. Dang's red pen.

Jordyn didn't answer right away. She was watching a kid across the sandpit hurling a ball for a dog, the arc of each throw hanging in the pink light. Something about the shape bothered her, or rather something about Sloane's word, pause, bothered the shape. A pause would look like a hitch, a hold, and she couldn't find one anywhere in the ball's flight. "Hang on," she said.

Emilee was already digging in her pocket. "I filmed like twenty of those throws yesterday for my photo project. I have slow motion." She propped her phone against a juice box, and the three of them leaned in until their foreheads nearly touched the screen. On the small display, the ball rose, rose, rose, and at the very top of its arc it flattened, for one smeared instant, into something that was still visibly moving sideways. Emilee scrolled frame by frame so they could watch it happen.

"It's still going," Jordyn said slowly, almost to herself. "At the top, it's still moving." She said it again in her head, turning it over the way she liked to, letting herself cogitate on it rather than rushing to the worksheet. Up had run out at the top, that much felt true, but across had not. The ball wasn't pausing; it was only pausing vertically.

"That's an oxymoron," Sloane said, defensive now. "The top of the arc and still moving. Those can't both be true."

"Why not?" Emilee asked. "Watch the frames again. Look where the ball is, then look one frame later. It moved. It didn't move up and it didn't move down, but it moved." She tapped the screen twice, left and right, tracing the flat little slide at the crest.

Jordyn pulled her worksheet closer and split the problem in two the way the diagram in the textbook hinted at, drawing one arrow for the sideways part and one for the up-and-down part. The vertical arrow she let shrink to nothing at the top, a candle burning down to the table. The horizontal arrow she left exactly the same length at the top as at the launch, untouched by all that rising and falling. Two motions, sharing one ball, keeping separate books. Was that true of everything, she wondered, or only of things thrown through the air? Did a stone skipped across the creek have a part of it that never touched the water? She copied the split onto Sloane's paper before Sloane could stop her, and Sloane stared at it, pen hovering over her circled zero.

"So my zero is wrong," Sloane said.

"Half wrong," Jordyn said. "Half of it's right. You just got the wrong half." It came out more pithy than she'd intended, and she softened it by sliding the pen across the table. The floodlight above the basketball court buzzed on, and moths began their spiraling work around it. Somewhere behind them the kid's ball rose again, and Jordyn found herself tracking the crest of every throw, checking each one for the sideways slide, wanting to see it with her own unaided eyes and not sure she could. She could believe the video. She could believe the arrows. Whether she could ever actually watch it happen in real time, she didn't know yet.

Ms. Dang came past on the path with her dog, nodded at their spread of papers, and kept walking without a word. Jordyn looked down at the two arrows she'd drawn, the vanished one and the stubborn one, and then out at the darkening field where the dog was leaping, the ball at the very top of its climb.

"There," she said. "Did you see it?"

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark chocolate, around 29-30 degrees Celsius, because milk fat softens the cocoa butter.
story:
The marble slab had cost Sophia's mother forty dollars at a restaurant supply store, and Nevaeh was afraid to touch it. "It's just cold stone," Sophia said, sliding it across the kitchen island like a hockey puck. "It wants to be used. It's lonely." Damien was already unwrapping the chocolate bars, a tower of dark and milk in gold foil, and Mr. Hoffmann, the chemistry teacher from down the street who had somehow been invited because he owned a thermometer, stood at the stove stirring with the gravity of a man defusing a bomb.

Nevaeh had watched eleven videos that week, and the number that mattered was thirty-one and a half. Dark chocolate came off the heat, got worked on the slab until it thickened, then went back over warm water to thirty-one and a half degrees Celsius, where it held its temper, shiny and decisive. She had written it on her wrist in pen. She had also, in a fit of ambition, promised her grandmother a box of tempered chocolates for her seventieth birthday, which was in nine days, and her grandmother was the kind of woman who noticed when things were dull.

The dark batch went first, and it behaved. Nevaeh spread it with the offset spatula, scraped it into a heap, spread it again, her shoulders burning in a way the videos had failed to mention. When the thermometer read thirty-one and a half, she dabbed a spoonful onto parchment, and ten minutes later the drop was glossy and it snapped when Damien bent it, a clean little crack that made all three of them cheer.

"I feel like a god," Damien said, eating the evidence.

The milk chocolate was for the shells, because Nevaeh's grandmother held a firm position that dark chocolate was a punishment invented for people who had wronged their families. Nevaeh ran the same route: melted, slabbed, worked, then back up to thirty-one and a half. The spoonful went onto parchment. They waited. Ten minutes passed, then twenty, and the drop sat there, tacky and streaky, refusing to become anything at all. Damien poked it and his fingertip came away with a smudge, like the chocolate had acceded to being finger paint and given up on being a candy.

"It's malevolent," Sophia said, glaring at the drop as though it had planned this.

"It's not malevolent, it's just wrong somehow." Nevaeh scraped the batch back into the bowl. Eleven videos, and every one of them had used dark. She hadn't thought to ask whether milk chocolate was the same creature or something with its own rules, which now seemed like an obvious question, the kind you only find after you're already sitting in the wreckage of it.

Mr. Hoffmann, who until this point had contributed only thermometer readings and one comment about specific heat, pulled out his phone. "May I?" He scrolled, frowning. "There's a chocolate supplier's page here. Says milk chocolate is usually tempered to a lower working temperature than dark, around twenty-nine to thirty degrees, because the milk fat softens the cocoa butter."

Nevaeh stared at her wrist, where thirty-one and a half sat in smudged blue ink, suddenly a piece of misinformation she had carried with confidence. "So I heated it past its own point. Of course it wouldn't set." She thought of her math class that spring, the way a curve could approach a line forever and never touch it, an asymptote of near-misses, and felt briefly that she had been living on the wrong side of one all afternoon. She cleaned the bowl without being asked, remelted, worked it on the slab again, and this time brought it up slowly, hovering the thermometer, stopping at twenty-nine and a half. The chocolate on the spatula caught the overhead light with a satin gleam she hadn't seen in the milk batch before.

The test drop set in under ten minutes and snapped like the dark one had. Sophia whooped. Damien clapped with flour still on his hands from somewhere, no one knew where. Nevaeh piped the shells into the molds, tapping out the bubbles, and set them in the cool of the garage, and when she came back Mr. Hoffmann was writing twenty-nine to thirty on a sticky note and pressing it into her palm without ceremony. She stuck it to her phone case, next to the photo of her grandmother, and went to check the ganache.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: A credit card's grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the full balance by the due date each month.
story:
The letter had come on a Thursday, and Colton had carried it around in his backpack for three days before opening it in the stairwell behind the gym. His father had signed the joint application without ceremony, the way he signed permission slips, and now Colton held a card with a thousand-dollar limit and a brochure full of words he only half understood. What he understood perfectly was the laptop on the second floor of the library, the one Zainab had, the one with the battery that lasted a whole seminar day. College started in six weeks. His mother's old machine died mid-essay in April, screen freezing on a half-finished paragraph about Hamlet.

He slid the card out of the paper sleeve and read the back, where the fine print shrank to something like insect legs. Grace period. Minimum payment due. He'd assumed a card was simple: buy now, pay later, pay a bit extra for the privilege. But the brochure used "grace period" the way his grandfather used "grace," as if it were a kind of mercy, and mercy, in Colton's experience, came with conditions nobody announced in advance.

In the cafeteria Monday, Yahia was spreading mustard on bread with the handle of a fork because the cafeteria had run out of knives again. "You got one," he said, nodding at the card, which Colton had set on the table like evidence. "My sister calls them traps."

"She also bought a car she couldn't afford," Colton said.

"That's not an argument. That's just her being her."

Zainab dropped her tray across from them. She worked weekends at the credit union near the plaza, the one with the fish tank in the lobby, and Colton had learned to bring her questions the way other people brought her gossip. He told them both the numbers: the laptop cost six hundred forty dollars, the minimum payment was twenty-five, and the statement said "due date" in bold.

"Pay the whole thing," Zainab said, before he'd even finished. "The full balance, by the due date. My manager makes me say it to first-timers. If you pay the full balance by the due date each month, you don't get charged interest on new purchases. That's what the grace period is."

"Twenty-five dollars is easier," Yahia said. "That's the whole point of the minimum."

"Easier is how they get you. Interest is what makes borrowed money cost more over time. You'd still owe the five hundred plus, and it grows."

Colton turned his water bottle in a slow circle on the table. In his head he ran the same arithmetic his father did at the kitchen table every January, when the heating bill arrived and the paycheck hadn't: what can we move, what can wait. He had eleven hundred saved from two summers at the garden center, money that sat in a savings account his grandfather had opened for him when he was nine. He remembered standing on a chair at the teller window, too short to see over it, while his grandfather said, watch, and the teller showed them a deposit slip with interest printed on it, a dollar and some cents that had arrived without anyone working for it. It had seemed like a magic trick then, and his grandfather had said, no, that's just what money does when you leave it alone. The opposite of what it does when you spend what isn't yours.

Mr. Otieno found him after last period, marking something in a red spiral notebook outside the science wing. He coached the cross-country team and seemed to know, without being told, when a senior was quietly recalculating his life. "You look like a man doing math," Mr. Otieno said.

"Sort of math."

"The kind with no right answer?"

Colton showed him the brochure, the fine print, the laptop flyer from his pocket, the bank app on his phone with its eleven hundred dollars. He said it out loud for the first time, the whole shape of it: he could charge the laptop, pay twenty-five a month, keep most of his savings earning whatever tiny rate the account paid, and feel safe. Or he could drain over half the savings, pay the card off entire on the first due date, and rebuild. "Yahia says savings are for saving. Zainab says the minimum is bait. I can't tell if I'm being careful or just cheap."

"Yahia sounds like an ideologue on the subject of buffers," Mr. Otieno said. "Fine people, ideologues. Terrible at arithmetic." He closed the notebook. "You want me to tell you which one's right. I won't. But ask yourself whether the money in that account is doing more good there, or doing harm somewhere else."

That night Colton sat at the kitchen table with the statements spread out, the way his father did in January. It was almost axiomatic in their house that you never touched savings, that the account was a wall you didn't take bricks from, and he could hear Yahia's voice defending it, and Zainab's voice calling the minimum a slow leak, and his grandfather's voice at the teller window saying, that's just what money does. Two rules that both claimed to be about safety. He circled the due date on the brochure, then wrote the full amount beside it, then crossed out the crossed-out minimum. His father passed through for coffee and looked at the papers.

"Decided?"

Colton squared the brochure against the table edge and typed the full balance into his phone's payment field, thumb hovering.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: The ocean stores heat from summer and releases it into the air in winter, and prevailing westerly winds carry that warmth onto northwestern Europe.
story:
Alex had forty minutes before the bus left, and the ocean current map in front of him might as well have been a painting of a snake. It curled out of the Gulf of Mexico, up the American coast, then bent east across the Atlantic in red and orange ribbons, and beside it a placid little card read that this current, the Gulf Stream, helped keep northwestern Europe warm in winter. He had been staring at it since the museum guide waved their class loose, and he still could not have said why. Mr. Ruiz had assigned each of them one exhibit to explain to the group before the return trip, and Alex had chosen the map because it looked easy. Nothing about it looked easy now.

"How's it going, ocean boy?" Paxton had drifted over from the hurricane exhibit, hands in his pockets, radiating the confidence of someone who had drawn the dinosaur hall and planned to say "big, then dead" and sit down.

"I don't get it," Alex admitted. "The water's warm over here, fine. But Europe's over there. How does warm water in the middle of the ocean warm up London?"

"Maybe it doesn't and the card is lying."

"That's not a theory, that's giving up."

Paxton shrugged and wandered off, but the question stayed with Alex, and that was the strange thing: it bothered him more than the deadline did. He crouched and read the map's legend again, then the smaller diagram beside it, a cross-section of the ocean with arrows showing heat moving out of the water and into the air. The ocean stores heat from summer, the label said, and releases it into the air in winter. He read it twice. So the water wasn't just warm in the tropics; it was a kind of battery, charged all season, spending itself slowly through the cold months. That felt like the beginning of something, but it still didn't get the warmth across an entire ocean to a continent.

Andrea found him there, notebook already full, because of course it was. "You look like an ascetic who's renounced everything except this map," she said, and he laughed despite himself.

"I'm missing a piece. The heat goes from the water into the air, okay, but the air could go anywhere. Why does Europe get it and not us?"

Andrea leaned in, tracing the westerly wind arrows printed faintly over the Atlantic, pointing east. "What are these?"

"Wind, obviously." Then he stopped. Wind. Prevailing westerlies, the caption said, and the arrows all blew one direction, off the ocean, onto the coasts of France and Britain and Norway. The wind picked up the released heat and carried it east, onto the land, the way a bus drops students off stop by stop. It wasn't the water warming Europe directly; it was the water warming the air, and the air making the delivery. The whole system sutures together like that, he thought, ocean to air to land, each part useless alone. "It's the wind," he said aloud. "The wind direction matters. If the winds blew the other way, all that heat would come back toward us and Europe would freeze."

"Ten minutes," Ms. Nkosi called from the lobby, tapping her watch, and Alex's stomach dropped. Ten minutes to turn a private click of understanding into something he could say out loud, in order, to twenty classmates who would rather be on the bus. He scribbled fast: summer charges the ocean, winter spends it, the westerlies carry the warmth onto northwestern Europe. Three steps. He could do three steps.

He gathered the group by the map, knees betraying him slightly, and began. "So the ocean stores heat from summer," he said, "and in winter it releases that heat into the air. And the winds over the Atlantic, the westerlies, they carry that warm air east onto the coast of Europe. That's why London is warmer than places in Canada at the same latitude." The words came out steadier than he felt. A hand went up, a girl from second period. "But why do the winds go east instead of some other way?" Alex opened his mouth and then closed it. He had no idea. The map just drew them that way, and the placard didn't say, and he hadn't thought to ask until this exact second. "I don't know," he said. "That's above what this thing tells me. Maybe it's about how the Earth spins." Someone muttered "smooth," someone else laughed, and Ms. Nkosi gave him a look that was half wince, half approval.

Walking to the bus, Andrea fell into step beside him. "The 'I don't know' was better than a fake answer, you know."

"Didn't feel better."

"It never does." The doors hissed open, and behind them, through the glass, the red ribbon of the current kept curling east, carrying its heat toward a continent neither of them had ever seen.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won and said 'we' more when describing wins than losses.
story:
The Ortiz living room smelled like chili and carpet cleaner, and by the third quarter every seat was taken, so Mason sat on the floor with his back against the couch, where the springs pressed into his shoulders through the cushion. Mr. Ortiz had invited the whole block over for the championship game, and Mason's father had brought a bowl of his mother's seven-layer dip, which sat half-finished on the coffee table next to Veer's sneakers. On the screen, the university team drove down the field while the announcers talked over the crowd noise, and outside the big window the arboreal street went dark so gradually that Mason only noticed when the porch light across the road came on.

Derrick was the loudest person in the room, which was normal. He had never played a down of organized football in his life, having been cut from freshman team and then claiming he'd quit, but he owned three university hoodies and wore one of them now, sleeves shoved up, veins standing out on his forearms as he gripped a throw pillow like it owed him money. When the receiver broke free and crossed midfield, Derrick stood up so fast he knocked over a can of soda, and while the father of somebody from two doors down mopped it with a dish towel, Derrick kept his eyes on the television and said, "We're moving the ball. We're actually moving it."

Mason had read something about this. It had been in a psychology article he'd found online back in October, initially for an essay on advertising, and he'd copied a line of it into his notes because it seemed strange enough to be useful later. The article said Robert Cialdini's 1976 study found that students wore more university clothing after their football team won, and that they said "we" more when describing wins than losses. He hadn't thought about it since, but sitting on the Ortiz carpet, watching Derrick's knuckles whiten on the pillow, the sentence came back to him whole, the way song lyrics do.

He decided to test it, quietly, because telling Derrick he was being studied would end badly. For the rest of the third quarter Mason kept a tally in his head, one column for when the team did something good and one for when they didn't. After a touchdown that put them ahead, Derrick said "we scored" twice and high-fived Veer, who had no affiliation with the university either except that his older sister had applied there and been rejected. When the other team answered with a long run, Derrick said "they can't stop that play," and then, a moment later, "our secondary is garbage," which Mason decided not to count, since it cut against his hypothesis in a way that felt like cheating.

Veer noticed Mason not cheering. "You rooting for the other guys or what?"

"I'm watching," Mason said. "It's a good game either way."

"That's a weird way to watch a championship."

Mr. Ortiz leaned over the back of the couch. He was a high school economics teacher, retired two years, and he had a way of listening to teenagers as though they were a market he was tracking. "Let him watch how he wants," he said. "Half the people in this room aren't watching the game anyway. They're watching themselves."

Derrick turned around. "What's that supposed to mean?"

"It means relax, it's third down."

The fourth quarter tightened everything. The university team led by four, then the other team kicked a field goal to pull within one, and Mason noticed that the room's language shifted with the scoreboard almost on cue. A big gain and it was we, all the way down the couch. A sack and the pronouns scattered like the crowd when a foul ball goes into the stands. His father, who had gone to a completely different college thirty years earlier, said "come on, we need one stop," and Mason felt something in his own chest pull the same direction, and he didn't know what to do with that. He had come in thinking he was the observer. The tally in his head had no column for him.

With two minutes left, Derrick started an argument with the guy from two doors down about whether the quarterback was better than a populist radio host kept claiming, since the host had been calling him overrated all season. "He doesn't know anything," Derrick said. "We're one drive from a title and this guy says he's a system quarterback." Mason watched Derrick defend a team and a player he had no formal connection to, wearing a hoodie from a university he'd never attended, and he understood suddenly that the study he'd read wasn't a criticism of Derrick. It was a description of everyone, or nearly everyone, and if it was a description of everyone then it was a description of him too, except that Mason had spent the evening trying to abrogate his part in it, standing apart as if watching was the same as being outside.

The defense got its stop. The room stood up in one motion, and the seven-layer dip nearly went over, and Veer grabbed Mason's arm and pulled him up off the carpet so that Mason was standing too, cheering too, saying "we did it" before he could think about whether he'd earned the pronoun. He noticed himself saying it. He kept saying it anyway.

Afterward, on the porch while the party drained slowly out the front door, Derrick came and stood next to him under Mr. Ortiz's yellow light. The trees along the street had gone fully dark, just shapes now, and somewhere a car alarm chirped twice and stopped.

"You were quiet in there," Derrick said. "Whole fourth quarter, quiet."

"I read this thing once," Mason said. "Cialdini, 1976. After the team won, students wore more university clothing, and they said 'we' for wins but not for losses."

Derrick looked down at his hoodie, then at Mason, and for a second his face did something complicated. "So you were sitting there grading me on my pronouns."

"I was grading everybody. Including me."

"You said 'we did it' at the end. I heard you."

"I know," Mason said. "I'm not sure what that means yet."

Derrick zipped the hoodie halfway up, though the night was warm. "Then I'm keeping it on," he said, and walked down the steps toward home.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The argument had started over the phone and migrated to the kitchen table, where it now coagulated around a bag of peppermints and a pot of tea nobody was drinking. Sasha had driven forty minutes to Anna's grandmother's house because, she said, texting about calculus was beneath them both, and also because she refused to lose.

"It's a maximum because the derivative is zero there," Sasha said, tapping the graph she'd drawn on the back of a grocery receipt. "That's the whole rule. Zero. Done."

Anna's grandmother, who had been pretending to shell peas at the counter, said that in her day arguments were settled by whoever was loudest, and that this seemed more civilized. Then she went to the garden and left them to it.

The problem itself had come from Ms. Ahmadi's review sheet, due Monday, and it was worth actual marks: a polynomial, a point where f prime of x equaled zero, and the question of whether that point was a maximum at all. Anna had said no, not necessarily. Sasha had said Anna was overcomplicating things in her usual way, which was the part that stung, because it was true often enough that she couldn't dismiss it. Sasha wanted the exam mark badly, wanted it the way you want something when your parents have started saying "we'll see" about tuition, and a wrong answer on Monday was not a thing she could afford to be casual about. That, Anna suspected, was the real reason she was here: not to settle the argument but to win it before it could cost her anything.

"Look," Anna said. She took a napkin from the stack her grandmother kept on the table, the thin kind that tore if you pressed too hard, and drew a horizontal line across the middle of it. "Stop thinking about the point itself. Think about what happens on either side of it."

"On either side of it is just the function," Sasha said. "I know the function."

"Pick numbers." Anna marked two test values, one to the left of the critical point and one to the right, and plugged each into the derivative. On the left, the derivative came out positive. On the right, negative. She wrote a plus sign above the line on the left side, a minus sign on the right, and sat back. The napkin looked like a very small, very earnest road sign.

"So?"

"So by the first derivative test," Anna said, and made herself say the rest slowly, because she was still assembling it herself, still checking it against the thing she'd half understood in class, "a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum. Because the function rises and then falls." She traced it with her pen: up the left side, over the top, down the right. "Positive means climbing. Negative means descending. It goes up and then it comes down. That's what a maximum is. Not the zero. The change."

Sasha looked at the napkin for a long time. She was quiet in a way Anna recognized from group projects, the quiet of someone recalculating, deciding whether to concede or to find the flaw. "Then a point where it's zero could be nothing," she said finally. "If the sign doesn't change."

"Or a minimum, if it goes minus to plus."

"That's it, isn't it." Sasha pulled the napkin toward her and copied the sign chart onto her own receipt, smaller, faster, as if compressing it would make it hers. "The zero is just where it's flat for a second. The signs are the actual information." She looked up. "Why didn't Ahmadi just say that?"

"She did say that. Tuesday. You were drawing a taxonomy of all the mistakes you planned to make on the quiz."

Sasha threw a peppermint at her, which Anna caught, which ruined the moment slightly by being impressive.

The screen door banged and Anna's grandmother came back in with tomatoes, and behind her, unexpectedly, was Nahla, holding her bike helmet and a printout of the same review sheet. "You two left the group chat on read," Nahla said. "Also I did the problem and I got that it's a minimum, so one of you needs to be wrong in a way I can watch."

Anna slid the napkin across the table and let the argument begin again from the top, this time with three test values, two tomatoes as paperweights, and her grandmother at the counter pretending not to listen while absolutely listening. Nahla read the signs, frowned, checked her own work, and found her error herself before anyone could point at it, which was, Anna thought, the only dignified way.

Later, walking Sasha to her car, Anna still wasn't certain about the last problem on the sheet, the one with a coefficient that refused to factor nicely, and she said so. Sasha shrugged and said, "Monday's problem, then," and drove off with the napkin on the passenger seat, where it slid sideways at the first turn and came to rest against the door, plus sign up.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed or dusted with powdered gold, treating the break as part of the object's history rather than hiding it.
story:
The bowl had been her grandmother's, blue with a hairline of white fish around the rim, and Nicole had broken it on the last Saturday of June while pulling it down from the shelf her mother had designated as safe. Three pieces. She had wrapped them in a dish towel and carried them out to the backyard folding table before anyone could suggest throwing them away, because she already suspected that her mother would be sanguine about it, would say it was only a thing, and Nicole did not want to be forgiven that easily.

She had looked up repairs on her phone until two in the morning, scrolling past glue and epoxy and a video where a man hid a crack so completely the bowl looked new. That had struck her as a kind of lie. Then she found the word in the corner of a forum, mentioned almost in passing, and read it three times to make sure she understood what was being proposed. She ordered a small tin of lacquer and a paper envelope of powdered gold that arrived in a padded mailer so light it felt empty.

Sloan came over on Thursday, cutting through the hedge the way she had since they were nine, and stood at the table with her hands in her back pockets. "So you're going to glue it and then, what, put glitter on it?"

"It's not glitter. It's powdered gold. And you don't hide the break, you fill it with lacquer mixed with the gold so the crack shows. It's called kintsugi." Nicole turned one of the shards in the light. "The break is part of its history now. My break is part of its history."

"Convenient," Sloan said, but she pulled up a lawn chair and stayed, which Sloan's skepticism usually did not permit.

The work was slower and stranger than Nicole had expected. The lacquer wanted to be moved in the wrong weather, tacky in the humidity, reluctant in the evening cool. She learned to wait for the hour after lunch when the table sat in the sun's first shade, and to press the pieces together and hold them longer than seemed reasonable, feeling for the moment the seam stopped wanting to slide. She ruined one fill by wiping too early and had to sit on her hands, literally, while Sloan narrated the whole ordeal. What she kept circling was the question of what she was actually restoring. The bowl, obviously. But also something between her and her grandmother, who was two years gone and could not see the fish or the gold either way. Maybe she was repairing her own record. She had started to think of the accident less as a sin and more as a peccadillo, small and human, though she wasn't sure she had the standing to decide that on her own behalf.

Ms. Santoso, the neighbour whose herb garden backed onto their fence, leaned over the boards on Saturday while Nicole was dusting gold along a still-wet seam with a fine brush. Nicole held her breath; the powder settled into the lacquer like something remembering its place. "You want less than you think," Ms. Santoso said, nodding at the brush. "It's a vein, not a stripe."

"Is that right? I've been worried it looks like I'm showing off."

"Maybe you are a little. That's allowed." Ms. Santoso picked a sprig of thyme she had no use for and put it down again. "My mother would have litigated that question for an hour. Whether mending counts if you're proud of the mending."

Nicole laughed, and the laugh almost ruined the seam, and Sloan said "breathe," and she breathed.

Adam showed up Sunday with iced coffees he spilled half of on the lawn, and by then the bowl was whole, waiting for the lacquer to cure fully, its three breaks running gold. He turned it and turned it again. "So if you'd dropped a different bowl," he said, "a cheap one, you wouldn't have done this."

"Probably not. Which bothers me, honestly. Why does the gold only go on the things we already decided were precious?" She ran a thumbnail along the inside curve, not touching the seam. "Or maybe the gold decides. Maybe you look at the finished crack and that's how you know what it was worth."

"That's circular," Adam said, delighted with himself.

"I know it's circular. I'm still going to think it."

Her mother came out at dusk with the porch light behind her, and Nicole put the bowl into her hands without a speech prepared. She had considered one, an argument about history and honesty, and had discarded it, because her mother would either see it or she wouldn't, and Nicole could not litigate her into seeing. For a long moment there was only the sound of the sprinkler two yards over and a moth investigating the porch bulb.

"It was my mother's," her mother said finally, in a voice Nicole hadn't heard before, not scolding and not absolving, and her thumb moved along the gold line where the first break ran from rim to foot, slow, like reading. Then she said, "Can we keep it on the table where people can pick it up?"

"Let's put it where I can see it from the kitchen window," Nicole said, and carried it toward the house, the last light catching the seam as she went.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Andrew Wakefield's 1998 paper in The Lancet claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was based on only twelve children.
story:
The house smelled of cabbage and old paper, and Chloe spread the two articles across her grandmother's table like cards she didn't want to play. One was the Wakefield paper from 1998, printed from a database at the school library before she'd left the city. The other was a review article, dozens of studies gathered together, the kind Mr. Hamdan had told them to find. He had assigned a critical review: compare two pieces of scholarship on the same question, and judge them. The question she'd chosen was whether the MMR vaccine caused autism, which her mother had said was settled, which was exactly why she'd chosen it, and which now, at nine in the evening with the deadline in two days, felt less settled than simply vast.

Her grandmother moved through the kitchen with a querulous energy, complaining that the lamp was too dim, that the soup was too salty, that Chloe had grown too thin. "You work too much," she said, setting down a glass of compote Chloe hadn't asked for. "In my village we worked with our hands and slept at night."

"I have to finish this, Grandma."

"Finish it, then. Eat while you finish."

Chloe ate while she finished. The compote was sour cherry, good, and she drank half of it before she went back to the methods section of the Wakefield paper, the part she'd skimmed twice and avoided a third time. She counted on her finger, then counted again. Twelve children. The whole paper, the one that had made her aunt afraid of vaccines for a decade, that had made headlines her mother still argued about at dinner, rested on twelve children. She turned to the review article and found its table of studies, rows of them, thousands of children folded into the rows. Twelve against thousands. She sat back and looked at the ceiling, where a water stain spread like a country on a map, like the steppe her grandmother described when she talked about her girlhood, wide and flat and hard to cross.

She texted Camelia. "did you know the Wakefield paper had only twelve kids in it?"

Camelia replied a minute later: "twelve?? my mom's whole book club is based on that paper"

"not based on it exactly. cites it. believes it."

"same thing to them"

Chloe typed "not the same thing" and then deleted it, because she wasn't sure it wasn't the same thing, or whether the difference mattered if the result was identical. That was the problem with the review Mr. Hamdan wanted. Not finding the facts. Deciding what to do when the facts pointed two directions at once, or when one direction was crowded and the other almost empty but wouldn't shut up.

She started drafting on her laptop. The first paragraph came out sounding like a Wikipedia article, so she deleted it. The second came out sounding like a lawyer, so she deleted that too. On the third try she wrote that the Wakefield paper and the review article asked the same question and answered it differently, and that any honest comparison had to begin with the sample sizes, because a claim built on twelve children could not carry the same weight as claims built on far larger bodies of evidence. She looked at the sentence for a long time. It was true, and it felt incomplete. Something about the twelve children themselves, their parents, the fear that had made the paper spread faster than any correction. She wrote: a small study can stigmatize a vaccine, and a million doses of reassurance cannot always unring that bell. Then she crossed out "unring that bell" because it wasn't hers, it was something she'd heard somewhere, and Mr. Hamdan circled borrowed phrases in red.

Outside, a car door slammed. Mr. Hamdan lived two houses down, and he was walking his dog past the fence, the little white one that pulled against its leash. Chloe went out onto the porch with her notebook.

"You're up late," he said.

"I'm writing the comparison. The Wakefield one and the review article."

"And?"

"I think I have a position. Mostly." She held the notebook against her chest. "The small study was wrong, and the big evidence is right, but the small study moved people more, and I don't know what a reviewer is supposed to do with that. Whether that counts."

Mr. Hamdan's dog strained toward a hedge. "What does your gut say?"

"That it counts. That I can't pretend the fear part didn't happen just because the evidence part is cleaner."

"Then write that. Say what's solid, say what's still uncertain. That's what critical means."

She went back inside. Her grandmother had fallen asleep in the chair by the stove, the newspaper folded on her lap, and Chloe covered her with the brown blanket from the sofa before she sat down and opened the laptop again. The cursor blinked in the empty paragraph where her uncertainty was supposed to go. She typed: what remains unresolved is not the science but the hold the smaller story keeps on people, myself included. Then she looked at it, and cut "myself included," and then put it back. The sour cherry pit sat on the saucer beside her elbow, dark and small as a swallowed worry, and she pushed it with her fingertip to the rim of the plate and began writing the next line.
